candidats.titre: How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances? -- by Charles J. Courtemanche
candidats.resume: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.

The first concerns the growing role of non-state providers, especially NGOs, and its implication for state’s capacity to deliver services and coordinate across providers. The second concerns the selection, motivation, and management of frontline workers who provide the services directly to beneficiaries. We argue that decisions about aid allocation and withdrawal should account for the but can quickly erode. need to preserve last-mile delivery capacity, which takes time and resources to build.

candidats.titre: An Odd Approximation of Inflation for State Dependent Pricing Models -- by Luca Gagliardone, Mark Gertler, Simone Lenzu, Joris Tielens, Al-Mahdi Ebsim
candidats.resume: We derive an aggregate state-space representation of state-dependent pricing models with random menu costs and strategic complementarities. The representation, derived from first principles, replaces the cross-sectional distribution of price gaps with a finite set of its moments (the first three), while preserving the key economic forces of state-dependent pricing--movements in the frequency of price adjustment and selection. Along the impulse response, inflation is an odd (cubic) polynomial in the average price gap. Embedded in a general equilibrium setting, the model can be solved by perturbation, filtered, and estimated with standard DSGE tools, and it matches well the global solution across shock sizes. Applied to the 2021--22 inflation surge in the United States and the euro area, it shows that much of the variation that linear models would attribute to cost-push shocks is in fact endogenous amplification through the frequency of price changes and selection.

candidats.titre: fereg: Fast High-Dimensional Fixed-Effects Regressions in Stata -- by Johannes F. Schmieder
candidats.resume: Regressions with many fixed effects are central to applied research, but fitting them to large datasets can be slow. In this article, I present the commands fereg and feppml, which fit linear and Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood regressions with high-dimensional fixed effects. Both commands use familiar Stata syntax and pass the computation to a compiled plugin. The plugin chooses among projection, Krylov, and multigrid solvers according to the structure of the fixed effects, checks every result before posting it, and runs on several processor cores. The commands support multiple and interacted fixed effects, group-specific slopes, regression weights, robust and multiway clustered standard errors, saved fixed effects, and prediction. Two simulated examples illustrate their use. In simulated designs with up to ten million observations and default stopping settings, fereg was 6–204 times faster than reghdfe and feppml 11–103 times faster than ppmlhdfe. The commands were also faster than fixest (R) and PyFixest (Python) in all 53 simulated configurations and than the Julia packages FixedEffectModels.jl and GLFixedEffectModels.jl in 52 of 53, with geometric-mean time ratios between 3.0 and 7.7. On administrative data with 1.2 million workers and 117,000 firms, fereg and feppml were at least 3.4 times faster than every other command at every number of cores.

Seven months earlier, Hungarian voters ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years in power . These political transitions, following years of increasingly centralised rule, raise an economic question that extends well beyond the two countries. Can smaller peripheral states still benefit from playing competing great powers against each other? Hungary, an EU member state, and Serbia, a long-time candidate, followed similar foreign policy strategies. Hungary called it “ connectivity ”; political scientists call it hedging : maintaining economic relationships with competing great powers, without fully aligning with any one of them. In practice, both countries continued to anchor in European markets while simultaneously cultivating ties with China, Russia and the US. For years, this geopolitical balancing act seemed to offer economic opportunities and leverage well beyond their size. The countries managed to attract investment, secure energy supply and even strengthen their bargaining positions. The downside of a hedging strategy, however, has not been made clear. Hedging might work as long as powerful partners tolerate diversified relationships. However, as competition among the major powers intensifies, playing all sides can become increasingly problematic. Les institutions de recherche, entre autres, se coupent donc d’un vivier de personnes compétentes, déterminées et passionnées. Cela invite à repenser l’inclusion dans l’enseignement supérieur et les organismes de recherche, en passant d’une logique d’adaptation individuelle à une logique de transformation institutionnelle visant une accessibilité réelle et durable. Le contrôle démocratique des services municipaux (eau, énergie, logement, déchets) s’est développé, mais il dépend souvent du bon vouloir des élus. Lorsque des villes reprennent en main un service d’eau auparavant confié à des opérateurs privés, l’interprétation la plus spontanée est positive : davantage de contrôle public, donc davantage de démocratie. Elle repose sur une idée simple : si un service essentiel redevient public, les citoyens devraient pouvoir suivre de plus près les décisions, demander des comptes et peser davantage sur les orientations prises. Concernant les cèpes, les poussées record que l’on a pu constater par le passé étaient notamment associées à une température proche de 13 °C pendant vingt jours. Cependant, d’une région à l’autre, d’une forêt à l’autre, on note de grandes variations. Les amateurs de champignons le savent : certaines années, les forêts regorgent de cèpes, tandis que d’autres, malgré la pluie, les récoltes restent modestes. Pourquoi ? La réponse dépend autant du climat que de l’humidité du sol et des interactions entre les arbres et les champignons. Ce que racontent les cèpes, partenaires discrets des arbres Le cèpe de Bordeaux ( Boletus edulis ) vit en symbiose avec les racines des arbres. On parle d’ectomycorhize. Le mycélium du champignon, soit un réseau de filaments souterrains, entoure les racines des chênes, des hêtres et de certains conifères. Les racines de ces arbres peuvent fournir aux cèpes, qui n’en produisent pas, une partie des sucres qu’ils produisent lors de la photosynthèse. En échange, les champignons peuvent, eux, transmettre aux racines une partie de l’eau et des nutriments qu’ils captent, comme l’azote et le phosphore, essentiels à la croissance des arbres. candidats.titre: Bien-être étudiant : le temps passé avec des amis compte plus que le sport ou le sommeil
candidats.resume: Des étudiants sur la pelouse du campus de l’Université James-Madison, en Virginie. Les étudiants qui passent davantage de temps à socialiser avec des amis, à participer à des organisations étudiantes et à des événements culturels ont davantage tendance à déclarer un plus grand bien-être. Taber Andrew Bain/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 , CC BY L’ESSENTIEL Une étude menée auprès de près de 80 000 étudiants états-uniens et canadiens lie leur épanouissement au temps passé en présence de leurs amis. Chez ces étudiants, le deuxième facteur lié au bien-être était le temps consacré au travail rémunéré et aux responsabilités familiales. Réduire le temps d’écran ne suffit pas : il faut aussi faciliter les rencontres en présentiel et soutenir des relations saines. Faire du sport, éviter l’alcool ou dormir davantage ne sont pas les facteurs les plus importants pour le bien-être des étudiants. C’est le temps qu’ils passent en face-à-face avec leurs amis et d’autres personnes qui est le plus fort élément prédictif de leur santé mentale, selon une étude de 2026 portant sur près de 80 000 étudiants que j’ai menée avec l’aide de mes élèves. Ce résultat a son importance, car les jeunes se rencontrent de moins en présentiel et communiquent davantage par le biais d’écrans. Entre 2010 et 2022, le pourcentage de lycéens états-uniens en dernière année qui déclaraient voir leurs amis en face à face presque tous les jours est passé de 44 % à 32 % . Dans ce contexte, les problèmes de santé mentale chez les jeunes sont devenus une préoccupation croissante de santé publique . Le suicide reste ainsi…

candidats.titre: La règle d’or budgétaire garantit-elle une bonne gestion des finances publiques ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL De nombreux candidats à l’élection présidentielle appellent à l’inscription d’une règle d’or budgétaire dans la Constitution française. En 2012, le Pacte budgétaire européen fixe en principe à 0,5 % du produit intérieur brut la limite du déficit structurel. Évaluer une politique budgétaire suppose aussi d’examiner ses effets sur l’activité, les services publics et le patrimoine transmis aux générations futures. Avec le projet de loi de finances pour 2027, la France fait face à une sempiternelle question : comment réduire le déficit budgétaire ? Une autre question mérite pourtant autant d’attention : quels effets les réductions de dépenses destinées à réduire le déficit auront-elles sur l’activité et les services publics ? Une économie budgétaire peut fragiliser l’emploi ou dégrader un service essentiel. À l’inverse, une dépense financée par l’emprunt peut répondre à des besoins durables. Le déficit budgétaire n’est donc pas, par principe, bon ou mauvais pour l’économie. C’est dans cette perspective qu’il faut interroger la « règle d’or » budgétaire : respecter une limite comptable suffit-il à gérer les finances publiques ? Une règle pensée pour encadrer l’endettement Dans le cadre européen, la « règle d’or » désigne la règle d’équilibre inscrite dans le traité sur la stabilité, la coordination et la gouvernance (TSCG), signé en 2012. Il fixe un objectif d’équilibre ou d’excédent pour l’ensemble des budgets des administrations publiques – l’État, les administrations locales et celles de la Sécurité sociale. Pour apprécier cet équilibre, le calcul retire…

candidats.titre: Gaz : l’Europe s’est éloignée de la Russie, mais accroît sa vulnérabilité aux crises mondiales
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La crise d’Ormuz a affecté les prix du gaz dans l’Union européenne, alors qu’une faible part du gaz importé par l’UE transite par ce détroit. Derrière ce paradoxe se trouve la profonde transformation du marché gazier européen depuis 2022, à la suite de la guerre en Ukraine. L’UE s’est largement tournée vers le gaz naturel liquéfié. Si le risque de rupture physique a reculé, celui d’une flambée des prix demeure. Au printemps 2026, la crise du détroit d’Ormuz a fait flamber les prix du gaz en Europe. Pourtant, moins de 10 % du gaz naturel liquéfié (GNL) importé par l’Union européenne (UE) transitait par ce passage du golfe Persique en 2025. Comment un choc qui frappe d’abord l’Asie, principale destination des cargaisons de GNL empruntant cette route, peut-il autant affecter les Européens ? La réponse tient à la transformation du marché gazier depuis 2022 . L’UE a réussi à se passer de l’essentiel du gaz russe acheminé par gazoduc, sans rupture majeure d’approvisionnement. Mais en se tournant vers le GNL transporté par bateau, elle s’est davantage exposée aux tensions du marché mondial. Le risque de rupture physique a reculé ; celui d’une flambée des prix demeure. Nouvelles portes d’entrée du gaz La recomposition est considérable au regard de la forte dépendance de l’Europe au gaz russe que nous soulignions dans une précédente étude publiée en 2022. Entre 2021 et 2025, les livraisons russes par gazoduc à l’UE ont chuté de 87 %, passant de 1 535 à 206 térawattheures (TWh). candidats.titre: À Antalya, une COP de « mise en œuvre », mais pourquoi et pour qui ? Le Nord ou le Sud ?
candidats.resume: L’ESSENTIEL La COP31 devait être une « COP de la mise en œuvre », mais dans les faits, les deux dossiers (financement climatique Nord-Sud et sortie des énergies fossiles) ont de nouveau concentré l’essentiel des blocages, dans un contexte géopolitique marqué par la crise du détroit Ormuz. Premier problème : la gouvernance climatique tend à réduire la crise climatique à une logique comptable, qui privilégie les mécanismes de compensation carbone au détriment d’une véritable baisse des émissions à la source. Elle place également les pays du Sud dans une posture où ils doivent être assistés financièrement par les pays du Nord, avec des prêts ou des financements privés qui risquent d’aggraver leur endettement, là où s’imposerait plutôt un dépassement structurel du régime extractiviste. Du 9 au 20 novembre 2026, la COP31 s’est déroulée à Antalya sous une présidence partagée entre la Turquie et l’Australie. Pour sortir de l’impasse politique entre Ankara et Canberra (aucun ne voulant céder sa place à l’autre), un compromis conclu à Belém lors de la COP30 avait confié l’accueil et la présidence de la COP31 à la Turquie tandis que l’Australie conservait la conduite des négociations. La pré-COP organisée aux Fidji et à Tuvalu (NST) n’a pas consolé les États insulaires, privés d’une « COP du Pacifique ». Les pays les plus exposés au changement climatique n’ont ainsi obtenu qu’une vitrine symbolique plutôt qu’une véritable place à la table des négociations. On l’avait baptisée la « COP de la mise en œuvre » : il s’agissait de s’accorder sur comment tenir les promesses de financement…

Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community said in a statement.
Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.
The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.
The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

SOURCE 2 (Scientific American) :
Editor's Note: This story was updated on Nov. 21 to reflect further confirmation of the proof.
Mathematicians are now certain the earth-shattering artificial-intelligence-created proof of the Riemann hypothesis is real.
On Friday Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the company’s Claude AI model to solve the Riemann problem, perhaps the most important open quandary in mathematics. The hypothesis, first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers—those numbers that are divisible only by themselves and 1.

Now researchers have verified that the proof does do what Alpöge claims.
"We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," mathematicians wrote in a joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, which support the Lean mathematics programming language. "We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct."
Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof using Lean; if a Lean-coded proof compiles error-free, this is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct.
But some questions remained. For instance, does the proof really address the Riemann hypothesis, or does it establish a subtly different point or idea? “The first question which one has to ask when judging a PDF which comes with some Lean code is: ‘what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement,’” explained mathematician Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London in a blog post.
A second question was whether the Lean code would successfully compile for other mathematicians. Independent researchers, including Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, have now separately compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean without issues.
“The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms,” Sutherland says. “Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.”
Researchers also made sure that the proof does not include any hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths. This process, called a “comparator run,” typically takes a matter of hours.
“We still await a successful comparator run, which will check that (a) the code does not do anything nefarious like redefine the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement and (b) (assuming it’s run in paranoid mode) the code compiles with several independent kernels (so the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean’s official kernel,” Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community.
That run has now been completed.

SOURCE 3 (shattered.io) :
A Riemann Hypothesis proof just cleared a test that no conventional math paper can pass: a machine checked every step. On November 21, 2026, the Lean Focused Research Organization (Lean FRO) and the Mathlib Initiative jointly certified that Levent Alpöge’s proof is correct, as the Lean community blog covers it. Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, built the work with help from Claude and released it on November 20 as a Lean library of roughly 17 million lines of code.
That makes this the biggest AI-and-mathematics story of the year, and it landed barely two days after publication. Inshorts flagged it as a top trending item on November 22. Our earlier look at who checks the 17 million lines asked the question the community has now partly answered. This analysis walks through what was certified, what the checks involved, what remains unconfirmed, and what it means for AI labs, mathematicians and the companies that sell AI models.
One caution up front. The certification covers the formal Lean and Mathlib verification process. Nobody has confirmed that the proof has been validated as a conventional mathematical proof outside that process, and this article keeps the two ideas apart throughout.
What Lean and Mathlib Certified on November 21
The joint statement is short and unusually blunt. The two communities wrote: “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.” They went further and added: “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct.”
Two separate claims sit inside that second sentence. The first concerns the statement: the theorem that the Lean code proves must be the real Riemann Hypothesis, not a weaker cousin or a mistranslation. The second concerns the proof: the argument must hold up under Lean’s rules of logic. A proof of the wrong statement is worthless, so certifying both matters as much as certifying either one.
The formalized statement carries the name RiemannHypothesis in Mathlib, the community-built library of formalized mathematics that Lean users share. That detail gives the claim a fixed anchor. The proof had to land on a named target in a shared library rather than on a definition the author wrote for the occasion.
The Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative both endorsed the statement. The Lean FRO is a focused research organization that works on the Lean proof assistant itself. The Mathlib Initiative supports the library that holds the definition. Between them they cover both the tool that checks proofs and the library that defines what a correct statement looks like. The Defiant reported the certification under the headline “Lean Groups Certify Claude-Assisted Riemann Proof.”
The Timeline: Release on Nov. 20, Verdict on Nov. 21
The speed of the sequence is part of the story. Many landmark proofs sit in review for months or years before the community reaches a view. This one moved from release to joint endorsement in a single day. The table below lays out the confirmed sequence, using only dates from the verified record.
We covered the first hours of this story when the claim was still just a claim. Our report on the Lean proof with zero outside checks described a release that nobody had yet tested. The November 21 statement changes that picture. Outside checks now exist, they came from several directions, and they agree.
Who Is Levent Alpöge, and What Did Claude Do?
Levent Alpöge is identified as a mathematician working at Anthropic. He released the proof, and reports on the project say he built it with assistance from Claude, Anthropic’s AI system. That is the extent of what the verified record says about the division of labor. It does not specify which Claude model or version did the work, how many sessions it took, or which parts of the 17 million lines a human wrote by hand.
Readers should resist filling that gap with guesses. Some commentary online already claims precise splits between human insight and machine labor, and none of it comes from the certification. The Lean and Mathlib statement speaks to correctness, not authorship. A correct proof is correct whether a person, a model or a team produced it, which is exactly why formal verification suits a collaboration like this one.
The State carried the story under the headline “Anthropic mathematician says AI helped solve famous math problem,” which matches the framing in the other coverage. For our own first-day view, see the earlier report on the four-page note around the first claim. The employer detail matters for a different reason. Alpöge works for the company that makes Claude, so the announcement doubles as a product demonstration, and that conflict of interest is precisely what independent formal checking neutralizes.
Why 17 Million Lines of Lean Code Matter
Seventeen million lines is enormous by any standard. Few human-written software projects reach that scale, and a formal proof has to be exact at every line. No reviewer will read all of it. A referee reading a journal submission looks for the central idea, checks the hard lemmas and trusts the routine steps. A Lean library at this size offers no such shortcut, which is why the verification had to be mechanical.
The size also explains the format. Alpöge did not post a paper with a few dozen pages of argument. He released a Lean library, meaning code that a machine can compile and a human can navigate with tools. The proof’s authority comes from compilation, not from a reader’s patience.
Here is the practical consequence. A formal proof of this size can contain many ideas, but the community does not need to understand all of them to trust the result. It needs to trust the small program at the center of the system, the Lean kernel, which checks each logical step. If the kernel accepts the whole file and the stated theorem is the right one, the conclusion follows. Humans can then study the structure at leisure, extract the key arguments and write the conventional paper later.
That ordering flips normal mathematical practice. Usually the human paper comes first and formalization trails by years, if it happens at all. Here the machine-checkable object exists first, and the human-readable account is the open work.
What a Formal Proof Actually Guarantees
Lean is a proof assistant and formal language. You write definitions and theorems in code, and a checker confirms that each step follows from earlier ones under fixed logical rules. If something does not follow, the file does not compile. This is a stricter standard than a journal’s, because a referee can miss a gap and the kernel cannot.
The statement check
A compiled proof only means something if the theorem it proves says what people think it says. That is why the two comparison tools matter. They compared the code’s stated theorem against the intended Riemann Hypothesis statement and confirmed that they match. Since the target is the existing RiemannHypothesis definition in Mathlib, the check also guards against a quiet redefinition of terms inside the new code.
The proof check
The second layer is the proof itself. Multiple independent proof-checking systems accepted it, including the official Lean kernel. Independent checkers matter because a bug in one implementation would not necessarily appear in another. When several programs written by different people agree, the odds of a shared flaw drop sharply. The record does not name every checker, and we will not guess at the list.
Formal verification still has edges. It guarantees that the conclusion follows from the stated foundations, and it cannot guarantee that the foundations are philosophically beyond dispute. Almost all modern mathematics shares those foundations, so this caveat rarely changes practical conclusions, but it explains why mathematicians phrase their confidence carefully.
How the Community Checked It in One Day
The confirmed checks fall into three groups, and each answers a different worry. Two independent comparison tools confirmed that the code proves the intended statement. Dozens of people compiled the code and reproduced the proof files. Multiple independent proof-checking systems, including the official Lean kernel, accepted the proof.
- Statement worry: does the code prove the real Riemann Hypothesis? Two independent comparison tools said yes.
- Reproducibility worry: does it build on other machines, or only on the author’s? Dozens of people compiled it and got the same proof files.
- Correctness worry: does the logic hold? Multiple independent checkers, including the official kernel, accepted it.
Reproducibility deserves more credit than it usually gets. A proof of this size depends on a pinned set of libraries, a compiler version and a build setup. If outsiders cannot rebuild it, the claim collapses into trust in the author. Dozens of successful rebuilds turn “it works on my machine” into a community fact.
The speed also reflects how Lean’s community works. Mathlib contributors already spend their days reading, compiling and refactoring formal mathematics, so they arrived with tooling, habits and a shared definition of the statement. No comparable infrastructure exists for informal proofs, which is the reason journal review of a famous claim can drag on.
What Stays Unconfirmed
Readers will see strong headlines, so the limits of the record deserve a clear list. The table separates what the verified sources support from what they do not.
The two unconfirmed rows carry real weight. First, a formal certification is not the same thing as acceptance by the wider mathematical community through papers, seminars and journal refereeing. The two will probably converge, but they have not yet, and anyone claiming otherwise is running ahead of the evidence. Second, no prize amount, release schedule or commercial product has been tied to this story. Posts that attach dollar figures to the announcement are speculating.
Historical Context: How Formal Proofs Earned Trust
The Riemann Hypothesis dates to the 19th century and concerns the distribution of prime numbers. It has resisted every attack since, which is why a claimed solution draws far more skepticism than the typical breakthrough announcement. Skepticism is healthy here, and machine verification answers it better than reputation can.
Formal verification has built that credibility slowly. Computer-assisted proofs started with controversy, because early readers distrusted arguments nobody could check by hand. Over time, proof assistants turned into the arbiters. The milestones below, drawn from general mathematical history rather than the November announcement, show the pattern.
The pattern across these entries is consistent. Each time, formalization moved a result from “experts believe it” to “a checker confirms it.” The Riemann Hypothesis case compresses the usual lag. Earlier formalizations of famous theorems took years after the original proof, while this one produced the formal object first.
Formal Proof vs Journal Review vs AI Output: A Comparison
Three routes now compete to establish that a hard result holds, and this announcement exposes the trade-offs among them.
- Journal peer review: slow, human and good at judging significance and exposition. It can miss subtle gaps in very long arguments, and no referee can read 17 million lines.
- Formal verification in Lean: fast to re-run, mechanical and reproducible. It checks logical validity with near certainty, but says little about whether the idea is elegant or illuminating.
- Raw AI-generated argument: cheap and fast, with a well-known habit of sounding right while being wrong. On its own, it proves nothing.
The Alpöge release pairs the third route with the second, and that pairing is the real novelty. An AI system generated or helped generate the argument, then a formal checker removed the need to trust the AI. Claude’s reliability becomes irrelevant to the final verdict, because the kernel either accepts the proof or it does not. For AI developers, this is the strongest available answer to the hallucination problem, at least in domains where the answer can be written as code.
It also shows the limit of the approach. Formal verification works where a problem can be stated in a formal language and where libraries like Mathlib already define the surrounding concepts. Most real-world questions cannot be stated that way. Math is the ideal case, and the lesson will transfer to software correctness and some security work before it transfers to anything fuzzier.

No verified source ties the certification to any stock move, and we will not invent one. The timing is still hard to ignore. Anthropic’s public debut was the dominant business story of the past week. Our coverage recorded that Anthropic opened above $2 trillion after its Nasdaq IPO and we reported that the stock closed at $97.17, up 17% over its $83 IPO price.
Against that backdrop, a certified Riemann Hypothesis proof gives the company a rare piece of capability evidence that investors can verify without trusting marketing. Benchmarks are easy to dispute, but a compiled proof is not. That asymmetry makes this announcement more valuable as a signal than most model-launch charts.
Caution applies in the other direction as well. A single mathematical result does not translate directly into revenue, customers or margins. Analysts who tie it to a price target are reasoning from a story, not from filings. The better reading is narrower: the result lowers the perceived risk that frontier AI systems cannot do original research-grade work, and it raises the bar for rivals who want to claim the same.

An open problem checked by an independent community offers no such escape hatch. Expect competitors to point their own systems at formalizable open problems, since a certified result earns attention that a leaderboard gain cannot.

Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users
Key Points
- Security researchers at Dragos exposed major security flaws in AI services using roughly two million test requests.
- Attackers were able to steal credentials and keys undetected for several months.
- Intermediaries and model marketplaces that routed the requests emerged as a major risk.
Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.
The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.
Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.
Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.
Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention" (ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.
Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.
OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.
Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.
Intermediaries are the weak link
AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.
Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.
Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.
"None of this means that you should stop using AI services. It does mean that where your prompts go is a decision, and if you don’t make it, the lowest price will make it for you", Chief Research Officer HD Moore writes.
A recent analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed how Chinese proxy services route requests to Western AI models like Claude through servers abroad. According to the analysis, those services can also read the requests in transit. It's still not clear whether the providers Dragos examined share any personnel with the Chinese proxy networks.
But the methods follow the same basic pattern. In both cases, intermediaries sit between users and the model developer, can view requests, and pass data on to third parties, often without users knowing. Data ends up with Chinese actors either way, even though users never meant to send it there, and privacy promises break down along the supply chain.

AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems," the organization warns.
On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.
The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

Règle d’or budgétaire : le texte de 2011 que Macron pourrait relancer
Emmanuel Macron envisagerait de réunir le Parlement en Congrès à Versailles en janvier 2027 pour inscrire une règle d’or budgétaire dans la Constitution. Cette piste, révélée le dimanche 22 novembre 2026 par La Tribune Dimanche et rapportée par Reuters, renvoie à un projet déjà voté par les deux chambres en 2011, sans avoir jamais été définitivement adopté. L’Élysée n’a pas commenté ces informations : aucune convocation du Congrès ni nouvelle règle constitutionnelle n’est annoncée à ce stade.
Selon le récit publié ce dimanche, le président aurait demandé au Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu de sonder les soutiens possibles, dans la perspective de la fin de l’examen des textes budgétaires. Le sujet est plus précis qu’une promesse générale de réduire le déficit : le dispositif imaginé il y a quinze ans liait les budgets annuels de l’État et de la Sécurité sociale à des orientations financières définies sur plusieurs années.
Ce que prévoyait exactement la réforme budgétaire de 2011
Le projet de loi constitutionnelle adopté le 13 juillet 2011 prévoyait des « lois-cadres d’équilibre des finances publiques » couvrant au moins trois années. Ces textes devaient fixer des orientations pluriannuelles, mais aussi, pour chaque année, un plafond de dépenses et un minimum de mesures nouvelles portant sur les recettes. Ces paramètres auraient été opposables, dans leur ensemble, aux lois de finances et aux lois de financement de la Sécurité sociale.
Le mécanisme envisagé ne consistait donc pas à exiger, d’un coup, que chaque budget soit à l’équilibre. Il cherchait à rendre contraignante une trajectoire pluriannuelle. Le projet prévoyait également des modalités de compensation des écarts constatés en exécution, à préciser par une loi organique. Ses articles 5 et 6 interdisaient l’adoption définitive d’un budget de l’État ou de la Sécurité sociale sans loi-cadre applicable à l’exercice concerné.
Autre verrou envisagé : le Conseil constitutionnel aurait dû examiner la conformité des deux textes budgétaires annuels à la loi-cadre avant leur promulgation. Cette articulation entre programmation, plafonds et contrôle juridictionnel explique la portée du texte ancien. Elle ne permet toutefois pas de connaître les seuils, le rythme de redressement ou les modalités que retiendrait une éventuelle initiative en 2027.
Pourquoi le vote de 2011 n’a pas suffi
La réforme préparée sous le gouvernement de François Fillon avait franchi les lectures parlementaires. Le dossier législatif du Sénat retrace notamment son vote du 11 juillet 2011, suivi de l’adoption sans modification par l’Assemblée nationale le 13 juillet. La version finale précise expressément qu’elle ne deviendrait définitive qu’après approbation par référendum ou par le Parlement réuni en Congrès. Cette dernière étape n’a pas eu lieu.
La distinction demeure essentielle aujourd’hui : un texte adopté dans les mêmes termes par les députés et les sénateurs n’est pas, à lui seul, une révision de la Constitution. Selon la procédure décrite par le Sénat au titre de l’article 89, un projet de révision peut être soumis par le président au Congrès après son adoption identique dans les deux assemblées. Il faut alors recueillir les trois cinquièmes des suffrages exprimés. La voie du référendum reste également prévue.
Le fait que certains partis se disent favorables au principe d’une règle d’or ne garantit pas l’approbation d’un texte précis. Le contenu des obligations, leurs exceptions éventuelles et le calendrier compteraient autant que l’accord de principe pour apprécier la possibilité d’un vote.
Une hypothèse de janvier 2027, pas une nouvelle contrainte en vigueur
Le débat sur les finances publiques intervient pendant l’examen des budgets. Mais le projet de Congrès évoqué par la presse le 22 novembre reste une hypothèse politique. L’absence de commentaire de l’Élysée ne constitue ni une confirmation ni une décision formelle.
Pour les ménages et les entreprises, aucun nouveau prélèvement ni aucune réduction immédiate de dépense ne découle de cette seule information. Les effets concrets dépendraient d’une éventuelle révision adoptée, puis des textes fixant ses conditions d’application et des choix budgétaires ultérieurs. À ce jour, le document le plus précis demeure celui de juillet 2011 : il éclaire le mécanisme envisagé, sans préjuger du contenu d’une réforme à venir.

Des villages du Pas-de-Calais sont toujours sous les eaux, dimanche 22 novembre. Des quartiers entiers ont une nouvelle fois été submergés au cours des derniers jours. "Ça devient lassant. On ne va pas vivre ça tous les deux ans", lance une habitante. Avec les crues qui se répètent, pour de nombreux locaux, une question se pose : celle de rester, ou partir pour ne plus subir. Avec leurs batardeaux devant les portes et trois pompes installées, certains pensaient pouvoir éviter l'inondation, mais la crue l'a emporté. "C'est passé par-dessus notre batardeau de la cave, je ne sais pas si vous vous rendez compte", glisse Isabelle Grenier, une habitante sinistrée de la commune d'Attin.
Des habitants à bout de forces
Dans le village, des retraités qui vivent au bord du fleuve de la Canche viennent de connaître leur vingtième inondation, celle de trop. "Là, ça recommence encore. Moi, je pense que c'est la dernière fois", ajoute Isabelle, livrant sa détresse et précisant ne plus avoir la force. "On va mettre en vente et puis changer de secteur", explique Raymond, son mari.
Il y a ceux condamnés à partir, et d'autres obligés de rester. En 2023, Geoffroy Quéant a eu 1,50 mètre d'eau dans sa maison. Depuis, il s'est adapté pour mieux se protéger. Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration needs answers from Nvidia as questions swirl about whether it has complied with export restrictions, after revelations surrounding its sent the chipmaker into crisis.
"We do need answers," Bessent said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
After Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO amid revelations about extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged spy, the U.S. is investigating how Nvidia may have given China access to advanced AI computer chips, despite government restrictions.
Last week, Bessent referenced a possible "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia, questioning whether the company was "pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings." In an interview on Fox News, Bessent said he needed answers from Nvidia on its compliance with export restrictions within 10 days. On Sunday, he told Brennan the administration has not yet received those answers.
"We've been in touch with the temporary management, with the lead directors, with their lawyers," Bessent said. "It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was."
Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, has taken the helm after Huang's departure. But Bessent has urged the company to bring someone in from the outside to run the company. The treasury secretary said Sunday, "We do need to see who was in charge of compliance there."
Asked how challenging it could be to get to the bottom of what Jensen Huang was doing, given reporting about Nvidia's "handshake" business approach, Bessent said, "For deals that size, there's no such thing as an untraceable handshake deal."
"There are bills ablating that movement, there are money movements," he said. "They may not be the 100-page documents, but it will be possible to understand what has gone on here."
On his call for an inquiry into whether Nvidia had a culture of noncompliance, Bessent said that it's simply a possibility that the dynamic was at play.
"We will see, and that's why I think the board is moving very quickly to establish whether this did or did not exist," Bessent said.
The comments come as President Trump has called for Jensen Huang to return as CEO of Nvidia. Asked whether the president understands the risks that Bessent has pointed to, Bessent replied that it remained to be seen "which level of the business knew about this."
"Was it at the lower levels? Was it at the middle levels? Did it go all the way to the top? And I have confidence that the Nvidia committees are moving very quickly on this and will come up with some very fulsome and robust answers," he said.
When pressed on whether he thinks it would be a good idea for Jensen Huang to return, Bessent said, "I think we have to see where the buck stops — Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?" He also drew a distinction between this possible dynamic, and Jensen Huang's alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy .
"I think that is kind of a canard," Bessent said. "Was there a culture of compliance versus one person's foibles?"
Jensen Huang has to testify before the Senate Banking Committee and will also be interviewed by House panels in early December.

Selon un sondage exclusif Cluster 17 réalisé en amont des élections générales espagnoles du 29 novembre 2026, le Parti populaire (PP), mené par Alberto Núñez Feijóo (30,4 %) est au coude-à-coude avec le Parti socialiste ouvrier espagnol (PSOE) de Pedro Sánchez (29,9 %).
- Suit Vox (extrême droite), mené par Santiago Abascal avec 18,4 % d’intention de vote et Frente Amplio (5,8 %).
- Il s’agit d’une percée extraordinaire pour Vox, qui avait obtenu 12,38 % des voix lors du scrutin de 2023, et qui semble avoir réussi à capter une partie de l’électorat du PP. La gauche recule également : Sumar, le parti de Yolanda Díaz, désormais fondu dans le Front large, obtient moins de voix que lors du précédent scrutin (12,33 %).
- La participation est estimée à 69 %.
- Si ces intentions de vote se confirmaient le jour du scrutin, le PP obtiendrait 125 sièges, le PSOE 120 et Vox 65.
- Avec 190 députés, le PP et Vox atteignent la majorité absolue, alors que le PSOE et ses alliés de gauche plafonnent à 150.
- Dans une enquête Cluster-17 de fin octobre, une coalition PP-Vox était toutefois jugée inacceptable par 54 % des personnes interrogées.
Le parti de Pedro Sánchez recule légèrement dans les intentions de vote (il avait obtenu 31,68 % des suffrages en 2023 et semble désormais bénéficier de l’affaiblissement de la gauche radicale), et faute de coalition viable, le Premier ministre en poste depuis 2018 pourrait toutefois perdre le pouvoir.
- Il s’agit de la quatrième élection générale pour Pedro Sánchez en tant que Premier ministre.
- L’un des derniers gouvernements clairement de gauche en Europe, il se distingue par plusieurs positions qui tranchent avec le consensus des partis au pouvoir sur le continent : une politique migratoire ouverte, une opposition à la hausse des dépenses de défense, une politique d’ouverture envers la Chine ainsi qu’un projet de croissance verte qui a vu un déploiement massif des renouvelables, qui atteignent 60 % de la production électrique.
- Sanchez est également parvenu à se maintenir au pouvoir sans parvenir à faire adopter de budget depuis 2022.
L’élection a lieu alors que l’Espagne a connu deux accidents ferroviaires majeurs cette année et que l’entourage de Sánchez est éclaboussé par des affaires de corruption.
- Selon le sondage Cluster 17 réalisé fin octobre, parmi les principales préoccupations des électeurs figurent le coût de la vie (47 %), la santé (43 %), le logement (38 %) et la corruption (37 %).
- La demande électorale est cependant extrêmement clivée. Les priorités divergent nettement selon les préférences politiques, la corruption et l’immigration dominent chez les électeurs de droite, la santé et le logement chez ceux de gauche.

Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
ANTALYA, Turkey – International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours with a disagreement over how to address fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
On Sunday, delegates from nearly 200 countries failed to reach an overall agreement covering targets for electrification, finance to help developing countries adapt to the impacts of climate change, and how to respond to the fact that the planet will soon breach a key warming threshold.
The talks ran two days longer than expected, becoming the longest climate conference in the history of these summits. And it ended in a dramatic fashion, with delegates from the European Union rejecting any final outcome that did not explicitly call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Some oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia opposed such language. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal makes up roughly 73% of global emissions.
Ireland's Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien, who spoke for the EU, soon left the room, along with EU Commissioner for Climate, Net Zero and Clean Growth Wopke Hoekstra.
Other countries also objected to the text, including Panama, Belize, and small island states such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands.
Hoekstra said that with the world heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been formal acknowledgment that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to try to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
Meanwhile, the transition away from fossil fuels is happening regardless of what the U.N. agreements say, says Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who ran the negotiations.
"The transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable," Bowen told the press after the agreement failed. "It's happening at speed and it's irreversible."
Disagreements on fossil fuels
The disagreements over mentioning fossil fuels in climate conferences have a long, fractured history.
The COP process works by consensus, so nearly 200 countries must agree to a final text at the end of the negotiations. Some fossil fuel producers like Norway and Mexico have recently wanted to include transitioning away from fossil fuels in the text. Other large oil-producing countries like Saudi Arabia and Russia have blocked adding fossil fuels to the final agreement.
At the climate talks in Dubai in 2023, countries agreed for the first time in 28 years of conferences to mention transitioning away from fossil fuels in the final agreement.
Deeply frustrated with this U.N. process, more than 50 countries have created their own separate conference dedicated to phasing out fossil fuels. In April, they held the "First International Conference for the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels" in Colombia. In 2027, Ireland and the Pacific Island nation of Tuvalu will co-host the second conference.
These side efforts are the best hope for climate action until something changes in the COP process, says Juan Carlos Navarro, environment minister of Panama.
"I am an optimist by nature," he tells NPR, "but I am not an idiot."
Increasing electrification
This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and the unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz loomed over the negotiations.
Since the war began, countries across Asia and Africa have accelerated their transitions to solar energy, batteries and electric vehicles, and reduced their reliance on fossil fuels like oil and natural gas.
COP31 organizers promised that this would be the "electrification COP." Climate technologies like renewable energy, super-efficient heat pumps and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Many of these technologies are being manufactured in China, the main exporter of climate solutions.
The conference's initial goal was to increase global electrification from its current level of around 23% to 35% by 2035. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra," Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember, told NPR when COP31 began.
The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was signed on to by dozens of countries. However, that pledge did not ultimately pass, says Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate change think tank E3G. "Electrification was collateral damage when the whole decision cratered," he said.
Lack of U.S. Presence
The Trump administration did not send a delegation to COP31 for a second year in a row. President Trump announced he would withdraw the U.S. from the Paris Agreement on his first day back in office in 2025. Trump has called climate change a hoax, and his administration has rolled back regulations on climate pollution and funding for wind and solar power and electric vehicles.
An informal delegation of congressional Democrats did come to Turkey. They told delegates at COP31 that when Democrats control both chambers of Congress next year, climate change will return to the main agenda.
Billions of dollars still needed
While the debate over fossil fuels stole the spotlight at this year's COP, a major focus of the negotiations has been on money. Countries debated new goals for funding to assist nations hardest hit by climate change.
Over the years at climate summits, lower-income countries have made the case that while they're responsible for only a small share of the emissions causing climate change, they're experiencing some of the worst disasters.
"We're not a nation that has the luxury of debating whether climate change is real for us," says Matthew Samuda, Jamaica's minister of water, environment and climate change. "The reality is, over the last five years, we have had a category 4 hurricane, a tropical storm and a category 5 hurricane. So climate change for us is indeed real and we are experiencing economic losses from a problem that we didn't create."
In 2024, nations agreed to eventually provide $1.3 trillion per year to developing nations, what's known as climate finance. Only about $136.7 billion was delivered in 2024, according to a report from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. The majority of that goes to projects that reduce emissions, including renewable energy like solar and wind.
As climate disasters become costlier, lower-income countries have been pushing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts, such as protecting coastal communities from sea level rise and strengthening infrastructure against storms. The United Nations estimates that those nations' needs will reach $305 billion annually by 2035.
During the talks in Turkey, developing nations pushed for more concrete commitments to deliver adaptation funding. But those elements to deliver on tripling adaptation funding by 2035 were in the larger decision that was ultimately rejected, Meyer says.
"Vulnerable countries from Africa and elsewhere are quite angry about that outcome," he says.
Earlier this year, countries requested $2.8 billion to help with damages, but only $342 million in funding was available.
At the COP31 summit, only $142 million in additional funding was pledged, far less than in other recent COP summits.
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.
Correction Nov. 22, 2026
A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.

ABSTRACT
Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known 
about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized 
controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in 
India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much 
capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that 
investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact 
statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and 
capital allocation.

MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 1
I. Introduction
The last two decades have seen tremendous growth in the scale and legitimacy of the movement
to combine social impact with corporate interests. Leading estimates suggest that impact investors
control more than one and a half trillion dollars in assets under management (Hand et al., 2024),
and that social enterprises generate more than two trillion dollars in annual revenue worldwide
(World Economic Forum and Schwab Foundation for Social Entrepreneurship, 2024). Impact
investing rests on the premise that capital should be allocated not only to profitable firms, but
also to firms that create social value. Yet this premise creates a measurement problem (Serafeim
and Trinh, 2020). Profits are measured because accounting, taxation, and investor reporting make
financial measurement unavoidable. Social impact, by contrast, is often costly to quantify, difficult
to compare across firms, and communicated through qualitative narratives. This raises a basic
economic question: are there private returns to measuring social returns?
We answer this question with two experiments. In the first, we randomize hands-on support
that helps Indian social enterprises collect stakeholder-level impact data and translate it into a
personalized impact report. Treated firms grow faster and raise more capital. In the second, we
randomize the impact information shown to early-stage investors and show that investors respond
to quantified impact metrics, but not to generic impact narratives.
We conducted the first experiment in partnership with Villgro, India’s largest incubator of
social enterprises. All 163 participating firms—spanning industries such as agribusiness, health,
energy, and education—were offered the same impact measurement and management (IMM) course.
Random assignment determined whether firms also received hands-on implementation support:
treatment firms worked through several one-on-one sessions with Villgro representatives to choose
an IMM framework, define impact indicators, plan stakeholder outreach, and operationalize data
collection; their customers, employees, and suppliers were then surveyed by the research team,
and the results were synthesized in a personalized impact report summarizing stakeholder surplus
measures.1 Control firms received the same course but not the full implementation support or
report until the end of the study.
The intervention had a large impact on both revenue growth and access to capital. Both groups
grew, but treatment firms experienced approximately an additional USD 20,000 in revenue growth,
bringing total treatment-group growth to nearly double that of control firms. Similarly, treatment
group firms raised an additional USD 43,000 in external funding, again a doubling relative to
1By surplus, we mean the value created for a stakeholder beyond the stakeholder’s next-best alternative: for customers,
willingness-to-pay net of price; for workers and suppliers, compensation or payments net of reservation values.
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 2
control. Our results are not driven by a small handful of outliers. We see a distributional shift in
both revenue and capital raised, and a statistically significant increase in median revenue growth
and additional capital raised. These findings document private returns to implementing impact
measurement. For social enterprises, faster growth could also expand the reach of products and
services intended to benefit customers and other stakeholders, thus potentially improving social
impact more broadly.
The intervention was designed to mirror how firms typically implement impact measurement,
and therefore combines several complementary components. This bundled design captures the
policy-relevant effect of moving firms from training to implementation, but does not allow us to
separately identify the contribution of each component or the specific mechanisms at work. The
intervention naturally creates two forms of decision-relevant information. Internally, the process
of choosing indicators, engaging stakeholders, and collecting stakeholder-level data may help firms
learn which customers and use cases generate the most value. Externally, quantified impact metrics
may make impact claims more credible to investors.
Access to capital is both a central outcome for early-stage social enterprises and a possible
channel through which impact measurement affects firm growth. We therefore run a companion
experiment that isolates investor demand for quantified impact information. We conducted a field
experiment with 223 early-stage investors with experience investing in Indian startups, inspired by
non-deceptive variations of resume audit studies commonly used in the labor literature (Harrison
and List, 2004; Kessler et al., 2019).2 Investors were recruited through Villgro and Harvard
Business School networks, direct outreach, and a professional survey firm. Investors were shown
hypothetical startup profiles, with characteristics drawn at random from the distribution of startups
participating in our first experiment. Investors then rated these profiles based on their investment
interest. Ratings were incentivized by the offer to introduce investors to real startups seeking
capital, whose characteristics matched the preferences investors expressed through their ratings.
Randomizing firm attributes allows us to infer the causal impact of any firm characteristic on
investor interest, holding other firm characteristics constant.
Our primary comparison of interest is how a startup’s social impact is communicated. Some
profiles reported only baseline customer demographics, such as average monthly customer income
and the share of customers earning less than $5 per day. Others added a qualitative impact
statement, meant to represent the narrative approach to communicating impact adopted by many
2For a related application of this experimental design to ESG impact signals in the labor market, see Colonnelli et al.
(2023).
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 3
social enterprises. Finally, others reported customer surplus, one of the key quantitative impact
metrics covered in the IMM course and implemented in the first experiment.
Our main result is that investor interest is strongly responsive to quantified impact metrics.
Moving a startup from below- to above-median customer surplus increases investor interest by
an amount comparable to moving the firm from unprofitable to profitable. By contrast, generic
qualitative impact statements have a small and statistically insignificant effect on investor interest.
Investors therefore do not appear to reward impact language per se; they respond to quantified
evidence of impact.
Our results contribute first to the body of work on impact measurement, impact investing, and
social entrepreneurship (e.g., Serafeim et al., 2019; Allcott et al., 2026b). Most related is the
work establishing a link between social impact and firm performance (e.g., Porter and Kramer,
2011; Edmans, 2011; Eccles et al., 2014; Henderson and Van den Steen, 2015; Khan et al., 2016;
Lins et al., 2017). Our main contribution is to provide causal evidence on the private returns to
implementing impact measurement. To our knowledge, this is the first randomized field experiment
focused on the implementation of impact measurement practices.
Second, we speak to the experimental literature on entrepreneurship training and management
practices (see Karlan and Valdivia (2011) and Bloom et al. (2013) for examples on micro-firms
and large firms, respectively, and McKenzie et al. (2025) for a review). Related to our focus, in the
context of micro-entrepreneurs, Kaul et al. (2025) show that customer feedback seeking can improve
performance and generate spillovers to customers not directly solicited for feedback. Specific to
startups, Camuffo et al. (2020) and Bailey et al. (2026) both find that entrepreneurship training
programs cause startups to more quickly abandon their ideas. We contribute to this literature by
studying the impact of a training program explicitly targeted toward high-growth social enterprises,
and focusing on impact measurement, demonstrating that this type of program can have meaningful
consequences for firm growth and the ability to raise capital.
Finally, we contribute to the experimental literature on investor social preferences. Existing
work asks whether investors value social impact and how they trade it off against financial returns.
For example, Humphrey et al. (2021) identify asymmetries between social benefits and harms, and
Heeb et al. (2023) argue that investors respond to relative, but not absolute, levels of impact. In
contrast, Bonnefon et al. (2025) present evidence that some investors have linear preferences for
impact that are symmetric between harms and benefits. Landier et al. (2026) argue that investors
value corporate intent in addition to realized social benefits, Bonnefon et al. (2025) and Green and
Roth (2025) characterize the degree to which investors have consequentialist social preferences,
MEASURING THE IMPACT OF IMPACT MEASUREMENT 4
and Allcott et al. (2026a) show that investor responses to sustainability disclosures depend in part
on how intuitively the information is presented. We study the information problem behind those
preferences: when impact is communicated in different ways, what type of evidence moves investor
demand? Our results show that investors respond more strongly to quantified impact metrics than
to generic qualitative impact narratives. Thus, the form of impact measurement matters for the
allocation of impact capital.
II. Experiment #1: The Impact of Impact Measurement
Our main experiment was conducted in partnership with Villgro—India’s largest incubator of
social enterprises. Representatives from Villgro, together with faculty from Harvard Business
School and the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, offered all 163 participating firms
the same impact measurement and management (IMM) course. The course was common to both
experimental arms, holding fixed exposure to IMM concepts, language, and certification. Random
assignment determined whether firms also received the remaining components of a practical IMM
implementation engagement: one-on-one support to select a framework, define indicators, and plan
stakeholder outreach; stakeholder surveys conducted by the research team; and synthesis of the
results in a personalized impact report. The treatment therefore isolates the incremental effect of
moving from IMM training to implementation, rather than the effect of classroom exposure alone.
A. Impact Measurement and Management Course
Startup participants were recruited through Villgro’s network. Active startups that had partici-
pated in previous Villgro programs, attended Villgro events, or otherwise indicated a desire to be
notified of Villgro programming were directly contacted to participate in the course. Represen-
tatives from Villgro also circulated several announcements of the course through its social media
accounts. All startups with a social impact focus were invited to apply to the program.
In total, 163 eligible startups (out of 277 complete applications) participated in the program.3
The two primary selection criteria were that the startup conveyed plausible ambitions to achieve

significant scale and social or environmental impact, and that a founder or member of the executive
team had committed to attend the majority of the course sessions, should they be invited to enroll.
The program was designed to build small and growing businesses’ capacity to measure and monitor
their impact, and participation was not limited to firms already incubated by Villgro. Our sample
spans the sectors and stages described below, but reflects self-selection into an IMM program; the
results are most directly relevant to growth-oriented social enterprises interested in improving these
practices.
The course ran in seven two-hour Zoom sessions every other week from April to June 2023—see
Appendix Figure A1 for the intervention and data-collection timeline and Appendix Section C for
the course overview.4 The course covered three main components that largely followed the content of
the Harvard Business School elective course “Data for Impact.” First, participants learned to outline
their theory of change, the mapping from their core business activities and outputs to societal or
environmental impact, and to make explicit the assumptions required for their business activities to
have their intended impact. Second, participants were introduced to three approaches to measuring
social or environmental impact. The Global Impact Investing Network’s (GIIN) Impact Reporting
and Investment Standards (IRIS+) framework provides standardized, sector-specific KPIs linked to
existing empirical evidence. Acumen’s Lean Data approach uses short customer surveys to capture
how products affect users’ lives. Finally, an economic approach based on customer, employee,
and supplier surplus uses willingness-to-pay, compensation, reservation values, and transaction
data to quantify value created for different stakeholders.5 Together, these approaches emphasize
direct stakeholder data and quantitative evaluation as the gold standard for impact measurement.
Third, the course covered tactics for communicating social and environmental impact to employees,
donors, and investors.
B. Intervention
Beginning in April 2023, treatment firms received hands-on support to operationalize impact
measurement. The treatment was designed to approximate a practical IMM engagement, in which
classroom concepts are translated into firm-specific metrics, stakeholder surveys, data collection,
and reporting. Each treated firm was assigned a junior Villgro representative and typically met

with that representative four to five times. Firm-specific, explicit guidance often included choosing
an IMM framework; identifying relevant impact KPIs; crafting survey questions and stakeholder
recruitment scripts; planning data collection; and synthesizing results for managerial and external
use. The Villgro representatives were selected for their expertise in impact measurement and
were instructed to interact with firms only on matters related to IMM implementation, rather than
providing general business consulting or strategic advice. They were also organizationally separated
from Villgro’s investor-relations team. The research team then conducted surveys of treatment
firms’ customers, employees, and suppliers and produced a personalized impact report summarizing
stakeholder surplus measures—see Appendix Figure A2 for an example. The additional support
was therefore specifically directed toward producing and using firm-specific impact information.
Control firms were offered the same course and certification but did not receive implementation
support, stakeholder surveys, or a personalized impact report until the end of the study. By July
2024, both treatment and control firms were invited to participate in a final round of stakeholder
data collection. At this final stage, all participating firms received an analogous impact report.
C. Data and Descriptive Statistics
Our analysis draws primarily on two surveys of participating startups.
Baseline data come from the applications that startups submitted to participate in the training
program. These data were collected in September 2022 and contain information on firm character-

employees, and amount and type of capital raised to date). The baseline application questionnaire

Our endline survey was collected in July 2024. It elicited revenues and profits for the previous

ABSTRACT
The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 
340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price 
Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the 
rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine 
possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to 
exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs. I also project the 
effects of switching the entire 340B program to a rebate model. I project net revenue losses from 
the RMP of $1.5 billion. Expansion to all of 340B would increase the predicted losses to $22.8 
billion, cutting net revenues from the program by 32%. The majority of losses will come from 
administrative and staffing costs, which do not benefit manufacturers, implying a net negative 
effect of switching to a rebate model. Covered entity losses from the RMP will be limited by the 
pilot only applying to a small percentage of 340B sales as well as restrictions HRSA’s guidance 
places on manufacturers. If the rebate model expands to all of 340B or if the restrictions are 
inadequately enforced, the losses will grow substantially.

I. Introduction 
The 340B program, created by the Veterans Health Care Act (VHCA) of 1992 (Public Law 
102-585), requires pharmaceutical manufacturers to sell drugs to “covered entities” at a discount, 
with the goal being to “stretch scarce federal resources” and enhance the ability of safety-net 
providers to provide unprofitable services. Initially, the law restricted eligibility as a covered entity 
to Disproportionate-Share Hospitals (DSHs) with a Medicare DSH percentage above a threshold, 
Federally Qualified Health Centers, and Ryan White HIV/AIDS clinics. 340B pricing only applies to 
drugs prescribed at covered entities’ outpatient departments and filled at in-house pharmacies or 
external “contract pharmacies.” The pharmacy collects the usual payment from patients and insurers 
and gives it to the covered entity in exchange for a dispensing fee. The entity then orders a 
replacement drug at the discounted price, keeping the difference between the two prices – less a 
dispensing fee when contract pharmacies are used – as its margin (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 
2026). 
Two major subsequent federal laws triggered substantial expansion of the 340B program. In 
both cases, drug companies were willing to agree to these expansions because these same laws 
benefited them in other ways, such as providing access to millions of new customers. First, the 
Medicare Modernization Act (MMA) of 2003, primarily known for adding prescription drug benefits 
to Medicare through the Part D program, also applied the DSH-percentage formula used for large 
urban hospitals to rural and smaller urban hospitals. This allowed many of them to clear the 
threshold required for 340B eligibility. Second, the Affordable Care Act (ACA) of 2010, which is 
best known for its large expansions of Medicaid and private non-group insurance, added critical 
access hospitals, rural referral centers, and sole community hospitals as new categories of covered 
entities.1 It also expanded eligibility indirectly, since state Medicaid expansions under the ACA 
 
1 Additionally, the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 added children’s hospitals (Courtemanche, 2026b).
