pushed many hospitals’ DSH percentages over the 340B threshold (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 
2026). 
HRSA’s revision of contract-pharmacy guidance also significantly expanded 340B. The 
agency’s original 1996 guidance limited covered entities to a single contract pharmacy, but a 2010 
shift removed that cap and allowed an unlimited number of pharmacies. This revised guidance was 
issued alongside the broader policy discussion surrounding the ACA and can be considered part of 
the bargaining process through which drug companies won access to a large new customer base 
while also avoiding a single-payer system (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 2026). 
Ultimately, the size of the 340B program grew from around $8 billion in 2010 (in 2025 
dollars) to $100 billion in 2025.2 Nonetheless, U.S. pharmaceutical industry profits rose from $60 
billion to $119 billion during this same time frame, outpacing the net revenues of hospitals, which 
grew from $84 billion to $94 billion.3 If one views the 340B program as a transfer from drug 
manufacturers to covered entities, this means that the program’s rapid expansion was essential to the 
hospital industry holding its net revenue steady in the face of other financing challenges. 
The rapid growth of 340B has triggered pushback from drug companies. They contend that 
the program is plagued by “duplicate discounting,” which can occur when drugs prescribed to 
Medicaid patients are eligible for both 340B discounts and Medicaid Drug Rebate Program (MDRP) 
rebates. According to the 340B statute, a manufacturer cannot be required to provide both the 340B

However, data fragmentation issues – particularly with Medicaid managed care – can make these 
cases difficult to identify in practice, leading to duplicate discounts being given in some cases. These 
challenges can also lead to diversion, which occurs when 340B pricing is given for ineligible 
patients – typically taking the form of a discount being sought by multiple covered entities for the 
same patient (Courtemanche and Garuccio, 2026). 
Since 2024, manufacturers have sought to move 340B to a rebate system, arguing that the 
existing system of upfront payments and inadequate data linkage does not allow them to prevent 
duplicate discounting (Hut, 2024; HRSA, 2026b). Covered entities have expressed concerns that a 
rebate model would give drug companies too much decision-making authority, create delays that 
could lead to cash flow problems, and impose substantial administrative costs (Courtemanche, 
2026a; HRSA, 2026b). Manufacturers were ultimately able to successfully lobby HRSA to 
implement an RMP for drugs included in the MDPNP, with the agency releasing guidance for the 
pilot in August 2026. Covered entities will no longer receive the upfront discount but instead 
purchase a drug at wholesale acquisition cost (WAC) and submit a claim to the manufacturer for a 
rebate (HRSA, 2026b). 
The MDPNP authorizes the federal government to negotiate the prices of selected high-cost 
prescription drugs with manufacturers. The negotiated prices are called “Maximum Fair Prices” 
(MFPs). The first ten drugs entered the program in 2026, with fifteen more scheduled for 2027, 
fifteen more for 2028, and twenty more slated to be added in each subsequent year (AHA News, 
2025; Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services [CMS], 2024, 2025). For 340B fills of drugs in the 
MDPNP, Medicare will only reimburse the MFP plus a small dispensing fee, lowering covered 
entity revenues. To help compensate, the statute requires that manufacturers sell covered entities 
4 
 
replacement drugs at whichever price is lower between the 340B ceiling price and the MFP 
(Courtemanche, 2026b; Santiago and Moldawer, 2025). 
Instead of building a real-time system to automatically apply the lower price at the point of 
sale, CMS relies on manufacturers to issue a retrospective discount or refund to the dispensing entity 
within 14 days of a qualifying claim (Smalldon, 2025). That retrospective, claim-by-claim 
reconciliation process creates a logistical challenge that ultimately led HRSA to agree to pilot a 
rebate system. Since HRSA created the RMP to be a solution to the practical problem caused by the 
MDPNP rather than a general reworking of the 340B program, it only applies to drugs in the 2026 
and 2027 MDPNP cohorts. However, the contentiousness of the debate raises the question of 
whether the RMP will remain connected to MFPs as the number of drugs in the MDPNP grows, 
expand to the entire 340B program as manufacturers prefer, or be short-lived as covered entities 
prefer. 
This study begins by providing a more detailed discussion of manufacturer efforts to push 
back against the growth of the 340B program, culminating in the push for a rebate model. I include 
an extended discussion of duplicate discounting, arguing that its prevalence is considerably smaller 
than manufacturer statements suggest, which has implications for the benefits of the RMP. The 
disconnect appears to largely be attributable to the drug industry using a broader definition of the 
term that also includes overlap between 340B discounts and rebates contractually negotiated with 
pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) who administer commercial drug plans and Medicare Part D. 
I then conduct a calibration analysis to project the impacts of the RMP on covered entities’ 
net revenues from 340B, holding all else constant. I also scale up these estimates to project the effect 
of implementing a rebate model for the entire 340B program. The analyses incorporate effects from 
both the rebate model itself and the fact that it will be implemented using the Beacon platform 
developed by Second Sight Solutions, whose parent company has substantial financial ties to the 
5 
 
pharmaceutical industry (Courtemanche, 2026a). Building off Courtemanche’s (2026a) study of the 
sources of value to manufacturers from utilizing Second Sight’s platforms and combining this with 
additional costs to covered entities identified by HRSA (2026b), I categorize these losses as coming 
from several sources: averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using 340B 
claims data for the purposes of influence, lobbying, physician detailing, and pharmacy targeting; 
costs related to cash flow and liquidity; and administrative and staffing costs. 
Using preferred parameter values, I project that these sources will combine to cause annual 
net revenue losses from the RMP of $1.5 billion, rising to $22.77 billion if the same model is 
expanded to all of 340B. Most of these losses will come from administrative and staffing costs 
associated with implementing the rebate model, as HRSA’s (2026b) guidance imposes restrictions 
on manufacturers that aim to guard against some of the other concerns. However, the impact would 
be larger if this guidance is ignored or inadequately enforced. Large losses – whether from low 
compliance or rebate model expansion – would raise questions about impacts on covered entities’ 
ability to provide unprofitable services and serve vulnerable populations. 
II. Background 
When the 340B program was created, administration was assigned to HRSA’s Office of 
Pharmacy Affairs. Since the VHCA gave HRSA little specific rulemaking authority, the agency has 
administered most of the program’s substance through sub-regulatory guidance rather than notice-
and-comment regulation. Manufacturers have attempted to take advantage of this ambiguity by 
imposing restrictions designed to reverse the program’s growth. This in turn triggered a flurry of 
lawsuits, with HRSA aiming to provide clarity where possible (Rogers, 2025). This section provides 
additional background about manufacturer efforts to shrink the 340B program and about the 
duplicate discounting that serves as the stated justification for these actions. 
6 
 
Beginning in 2020, Eli Lilly, AstraZeneca, Sanofi, Novartis, Novo Nordisk, and eventually 
over 20 other manufacturers began restricting 340B pricing on shipments to contract pharmacies. For 
instance, AstraZeneca would recognize only one contract pharmacy absent an in-house pharmacy, 
Sanofi and Novo Nordisk allowed more only if the covered entity supplied 340B claims data, United 
Therapeutics stopped recognizing contract pharmacies added after the third quarter of 2020, and 
Novartis limited recognition to pharmacies within 40 miles of the covered entity (Courtemanche and 
Garuccio, 2026). 
HRSA responded with an advisory opinion in December 2020 declaring the restrictions 
unlawful, which led to a wave of manufacturer lawsuits (U.S. Department of Health and Human 
Services, Office of the General Counsel, 2020). In AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Becerra 
(2023), the Third Circuit held that the 340B statute does not require manufacturers to ship to an 
unlimited number of contract pharmacies. The D.C. Circuit reached a similar conclusion in May 
2024, ruling for Novartis and United Therapeutics in a consolidated case (Novartis Pharmaceuticals 
Corp. v. Johnson, 2024). These rulings in favor of manufacturers, combined with HRSA's inability 
to force compliance, spurred state legislatures to act. By August 2025, 18 states had enacted laws 
protecting contract pharmacy networks against manufacturer restrictions (ASHP News, 2025). 
Manufacturers challenged the first of these laws, Arkansas’s, but the Eighth Circuit upheld it in 
2024, ruling that Congress’ silence on contract-pharmacy distribution left room for state regulation 
(Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America v. McClain, 2024). 
Manufacturers have also increasingly required covered entities and contract pharmacies to 
route their claims data through third-party compliance platforms before 340B pricing is honored. 
The dominant platform, the Enhanced Services Platform (“ESP”), was developed by Second Sight 
Solutions, LLC. Courtemanche (2026a) documents that this company’s parent company, Berkeley 
7 
 
Research Group, has extensive ties to the pharmaceutical industry, raising conflict of interest 
questions. 
Manufacturers’ attempt to switch the 340B program from an upfront discount model to a 
rebate model represents the next step in their fight to reduce their forgone revenue from the program. 
This strategy dates back to August 2024, when Johnson & Johnson announced that a new platform 
by Second Sight, Beacon Channel Management, would administer 340B pricing for DSH hospitals 
purchasing Stelara and Xarelto as a rebate rather than a point-of-sale discount (Hut, 2024). HRSA 
directed the company to withdraw the plan, asserting that a manufacturer cannot unilaterally impose 
a rebate model without HHS approval (American Hospital Association, 2024). Johnson & Johnson 
unsuccessfully sued HHS and HRSA in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, while a 
related challenge by Novartis, Eli Lilly, and Bristol Myers Squibb reached the same result on appeal 
(America’s Essential Hospitals, 2025). Together, these rulings established that an HRSA-approved 
channel would be necessary for a rebate model to move forward. This is exactly what happened next 
with HRSA’s rebate pilot. 
The process leading to the RMP began with HRSA opening an application process for 
manufacturers in mid-2025. By November, the agency had approved rebate plans from the 
manufacturers of all ten first-cohort MFP drugs (Eyman Partners, 2025). The American Hospital 
Association sued the Department of Health and Human Services and obtained a preliminary 
injunction blocking the pilot just before its planned effective date. This was upheld by the First 
Circuit Court of Appeals (Pease Bell, 2026). HRSA subsequently issued a revised version of the 
pilot via Federal Register notice on August 3, 2026 (HRSA, 2026b), with hospital groups signaling 
possible further legal challenges (American Hospital Association, 2026). 
Manufacturers have consistently framed these actions as protecting against duplicate 
discounting and diversion. In its July 2020 letter to HRSA justifying its contract-pharmacy policy, 
8 
 
AstraZeneca cited “significant increases in covered entity violations of the statutory prohibitions 
against product diversion and duplicate discounting” (AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals LP v. Becerra, 
Complaint, 2021). Eli Lilly offered a similar rationale for its claims-data requirement, stating that the 
data collection was “intended to stop the rampant fraud, waste, and abuse in the 340B program that 
is harming employers, state and federal governments, and patients,” and that manufacturers “can 
lawfully collect this claims data to detect fraud, abuse, and unlawful duplicate discounts” (Eli Lilly 
and Company, 2026). PhRMA has advanced the same justification for the rebate model, arguing in 
an April 2026 comment letter to HRSA that the pilot not initially being implemented left 
manufacturers with no way to prevent duplicate 340B and Medicaid discounts, that a rebate model 
“could directly benefit patients by encouraging 340B patient identification at the pharmacy or point 
of administration,” and that payers, manufacturers, and the public “are no longer obligated to 
shoulder the ever-increasing costs of rampant 340B program violations” (Pharmaceutical Research 
and Manufacturers of America, 2026). 
However, a closer look reveals that the evidence does not support claims of widespread 
statutory duplicate discounting, and that manufacturers’ interest in claims data and a rebate model 
likely reflects additional sources of value. Based on results from HRSA audits of covered entities 
combined with information on the share of Medicaid patients, Courtemanche (2026a) estimates that 
$1.9 billion of 340B purchases nationally (a relatively modest 2.3% of the annual total of $81.4 
billion) end up receiving duplicate discounts from 340B/Medicaid overlap while diversion occurs for 
an additional $1.22 billion (1.5%). The actual additional revenue pharmaceutical companies would 
make if these errors were corrected is less than these amounts, which represent the aggregate 
purchase price of all units bought with the 340B discount rather than the size of the erroneous 
discounts. In contrast, Courtemanche (2026a) estimates that other sources of value that full 
utilization of Second Sight’s platforms would create for manufacturers – including from avoiding 
9 
 
payment on valid 340B claims, building derivative data products for lobbying purposes, using the 
data to target and influence individual health care providers, and licensing the data – totals a much 
more substantial $9.33 billion per year. 
The gap between industry statements regarding duplicate discounting and the available 
evidence can be largely explained by differences in how duplicate discounting is defined. The 340B 
statute only defines duplicate discounting as the combination of a 340B discount with an MDRP 
rebate (Public Law 102-585, 42 U.S.C. § 256b(a)(5)(A)(i)). 340B discounts can occur alongside 
other discounts or rebates given by drug manufacturers, but there is no statutory basis for denying 
340B claims in such cases. For instance, in both commercial insurance and Medicare Part D, 
pharmacy benefit managers commonly negotiate confidential rebates with drug manufacturers in 
exchange for favorable formulary placement, which could include preferred tier status, absence of 
prior authorization, or preferred positioning over a competitor. These rebates are typically paid after 
the point of sale, often quarterly, and are not visible to the pharmacy or patient (Coster, 2025). 
When a drug subject to such a rebate also receives a 340B discount, manufacturers consider 
this duplicate discounting, even though it is not characterized as such by the law. A white paper by 
IQVIA – a company whose customer base is mostly drug and biotech companies (Umbrex, 2026) – 
makes this clear by stating that “products dispensed to a 340B patient, should not be subject to a 
payor (commercial or state) rebate,” and describing such rebates as resulting in “significant financial 
losses for manufacturers” (Singh, 2023, pp. 3–4). Using the expansive definition of duplicate 
discounting favored by the pharmaceutical industry, IQVIA estimates it to be $34 to $37.5 billion 
per year (Singh, 2023), representing almost 30% of the study’s estimated size of 340B.4 As a percent 
of the program, this is about 13 times larger than Courtemanche’s (2026a) estimate. This stark 
difference is not surprising; whereas the statutory definition limits duplicate discounting to

Medicaid, which covers only 18% of the U.S. population, the expansive definition also includes 
commercial insurance (66%) and Medicare (19%) (Bunch and Ketema, 2025).

Administrative and Staffing Costs

27 
 
 
IV. Conclusion 
For drugs in the MDPNP, 340B covered entities are eligible for the lower of the MFP and 
340B ceiling price. The lack of a system to identify and charge the lower price in real time creates 
implementation challenges. This, combined with longstanding manufacturer concerns about 
duplicate discounting, led HRSA to develop a pilot to implement a 340B rebate model for MDPNP 
drugs. Covered entities have objected to the RMP due to concerns about drug companies being given 
the power to approve or deny claims, cash flow challenges from delayed payments, administrative 
costs, and the conflict of interest created by the RMP’s claims submission platform being run by a 
company with connections to the pharmaceutical industry. After legal challenges, HRSA released an 
official notice for a revised version of the pilot that aims to address some of these concerns in 
August 2026. This study asks two questions. First, how will the RMP affect covered entities’ net 
revenues from the 340B program? Second, what would be the impact of implementing the same 
rebate model for all of 340B, rather than just the 22 drugs in the first two MDPNP cohorts? 
I begin with a section that provides background information about manufacturers’ efforts to 
push back against the growth of the 340B program. I examine the premise behind these efforts: that 
duplicate discounting by covered entities is widespread. I argue that a major source of the gap 
between industry statements and the available evidence is that drug companies define duplicate 
discounting much more broadly than the 340B statute. Courtemanche (2026a) suggests that 

28 
 
manufacturers’ interest in the rebate model likely extends beyond preventing statutory duplicate 
discounting, as requiring covered entities to submit claims data through an industry-connected 
platform creates other sources of value that are much more substantial than the benefit from stopping 
duplicate discounting by the statutory definition. 
I then turn to the quantitative analyses, allowing effects to come both from the rebate model 
itself and manufacturers’ ability to use the data collected to implement it in ways that can shrink the 
340B program. More specifically, covered entity losses can come from averted duplicate discounts; 
denial of valid claims; manufacturers using 340B claims data for the purposes of influence, 
lobbying, physician detailing, and pharmacy targeting; costs related to cash flow and liquidity; and 
administrative and staffing costs. Based on preferred parameter values, I estimate annual net revenue 
losses of $1.5 billion from the RMP and $22.77 billion from expanding the rebate model to the full 
program. The majority of these losses will come from administrative and staffing costs, but losses 
from other sources have the potential to be much higher if HRSA’s guidance for manufacturers is 
ignored, not enforced, or not included in a scaled-up rebate model. One specific concern is that 
compliance may be high during the initial pilot period as manufacturers aim to convince HRSA that 
the rebate model is working, but then worsen once the model has expanded beyond the point where 
it would be impossible to reverse. 
Losses of $22.77 billion would eliminate 32% of net revenues from 340B and, strikingly, 
24% of the combined net revenues of all hospitals in the U.S.6 Losses of this magnitude have the 
potential to significantly affect access to care. In their review of the scholarly literature on 340B, 
Courtemanche and Garuccio (2026) document substantial evidence that covered entities use at least 
some of their 340B revenue to maintain or expand provision of services to vulnerable populations. 
According to the Chartis Center for Rural Health (2026), 417 rural hospitals are vulnerable to 
 
6 24% is based on the calculation in footnote 3 that annual hospital net revenues total $94 billion. 
29 
 
closure, 448 have dropped chemotherapy in the past decade, and 331 have dropped obstetrics. 
Therefore, a loss of 340B net revenue of the magnitude found in this study would likely lead to 
closures of unprofitable departments and, in some cases, entire hospitals. 
Adding to the concern are two other developments that have the potential to substantially 
harm covered entity finances. The first is the MDPNP itself, which lowers covered entity costs when 
MFPs are below the 340B ceiling price but reduces revenues by lowering Medicare reimbursement 
rates to MFP plus a dispensing fee, which in turn will likely trigger a downward adjustment in 
commercial rates. Courtemanche (2026b) computes that the revenue reduction – which occurs across 
a broader base of drugs and payers – will far outweigh the cost reduction, harming covered entity 
finances on net. 
Second, CMS has proposed a 2027 Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) rule that 
would reduce 340B Part B hospital reimbursement from 6% above average sales price to 33.4% 
below. CMS estimates a $4.55 billion reduction in Medicare drug payments from this change, which 
means an equivalent reduction in covered entity revenue. This would be accompanied by a budget-
neutral increase in non-drug OPPS payments that would be spread across all OPPS hospitals, 
whereas only covered entities would bear the losses (CMS, 2026). 
These other developments highlight the importance of viewing the challenges facing covered 
entities holistically rather than separately. Unfortunately, it is not feasible with available data to 
develop a single comprehensive model that incorporates the interactive effects of these different 
forces. The impacts predicted by my analysis were computed in “all else equal” fashion based on a 
2025 baseline. Changes to payment rules would inevitably influence effect sizes. With that said, this 
influence is somewhat limited by three factors. First, since Part B drugs were not included in the 
2026 and 2027 MDPNP cohorts, the proposed OPPS payment changes are not relevant for the 
projections about the RMP – though they are for the projections about switching the entire 340B 
30 
 
program to a rebate model. Second, conversely, MDPNP payment changes are relevant for the RMP 
but not for extrapolation to the rest of the 340B program, as drugs not in the MDPNP are unaffected. 
Third, there is considerable policy uncertainty surrounding whether the OPPS changes will be 
implemented, whether the MDPNP will expand as planned, and whether the rebate model will scale 
up with the MDPNP if it does. Therefore, it is unclear whether incorporating all these potential 
changes into a single model would be desirable even if it were feasible. 
Modeling details aside, the fact that the 340B program faces pressures from several 
directions underscores the importance of taking a holistic view of these challenges when evaluating 
the merits of any single revenue-reducing policy change. To illustrate, when viewed in isolation, one 
might argue that covered entity losses from the RMP are relatively modest. However, this argument 
becomes weaker once observers recognize that covered entities face multiple forces putting 
substantial downward pressure on 340B net revenue. When viewed in this manner, even seemingly 
modest losses from the RMP could be consequential for safety-net providers struggling to remain 
financially viable. Similarly, once the pressures covered entities already face from the MDPNP and 
potential expansion of the rebate model is understood, implementing the OPPS rate cuts may appear 
less desirable. Alternatively, policymakers could consider offsetting covered entities’ losses with an 
additional policy lever such as increased disproportionate share funds. While identifying the ideal 
bundle of policies is beyond the scope of this paper, taking a holistic view would give policymakers 
a better chance of achieving their objectives while minimizing unintended consequences. 
Another relevant aspect of this study’s results for optimal policy is that the majority of 
projected losses from the rebate model come from administrative and staffing costs. In contrast to 
other sources of losses such as averted duplicate discounting, drug manufacturers do not benefit 
when covered entities incur higher administrative and staffing costs. This means that manufacturer 
gains from the RMP are smaller than covered entity losses, implying a negative net effect of the 
31 
 
rebate model. In a full social welfare calculation, employment created by the added administrative 
work would be counted as an offsetting force, but employment effects are not an objective of the 
RMP and would not be expected to outweigh the efficiency loss. 
The analyses in this paper also have implications for the broader policy debate over 340B. 
First, because the program faces several simultaneous revenue pressures, evaluating each policy 
change in isolation is likely to understate its consequences for covered entities and the populations 
they serve. Second, the distinction between statutory and non-statutory duplicate discounting matters 
for interpreting prevalence estimates. HRSA’s (2026b) guidance cites statistics from pharmaceutical-
industry-funded studies using the expansive definition of duplicate discounting, which my analysis 
suggests overstates the prevalence of statutory duplicate discounting by an order of magnitude. It 
seems unlikely that HRSA’s citation of these numbers was meant to give tacit approval of the 
expansive definition, as the agency has always clearly defined duplicate discounting in the statutory 
sense. Instead, HRSA likely quoted these numbers simply because they are the most publicized 
estimates. Independent, transparent estimates based on the statutory definition would help inform 
this debate. For instance, HRSA reports results from its audits in terms of the percentage of covered 
entities with at least one violation; releasing information on the extent of the violations where at least 
one occurs would be more informative. 
Finally, if it becomes clear that the rebate model will become permanent – either for just 
MDPNP drugs or for the entire 340B program – attention should go towards minimizing its costs. 
This takes two forms. First, the estimates in this study depend critically on the extent to which 
HRSA’s restrictions on manufacturers are followed and enforced. Policymakers should therefore 
prioritize monitoring and enforcement of these restrictions and ensure that comparable safeguards 
accompany any expansion of the rebate model. Second, because administrative and staffing costs 
account for most of the projected losses, policymakers could consider offsetting them through 
32 
 
government or manufacturer funding or modifying implementation details to reduce them. The 340B 
program is at a critical juncture, and the cumulative effects of these policy changes on safety-net 
providers warrant careful consideration.

Thomas Saunier, directeur général de Malakoff Humanis, a été démis de ses fonctions. Il est visé, depuis plusieurs mois, par une enquête du PNF pour corruption.
Malakoff Humanis se sépare de Thomas Saunier. Le groupe de protection sociale a décidé de mettre fin aux fonctions, vendredi 20 novembre, de son directeur général, en poste depuis dix ans. C'est le conseil d'administration qui a acté cette décision, "décidée à l'unanimité", dans un climat d'agitation après l'ouverture d'une enquête contre le patron de Malakoff Humanis. "Nous savons que les derniers mois ont pu être éprouvants et générer des interrogations, parfois de l'inquiétude", indique le groupe.
Thomas Saunier est dans le viseur du Parquet national financier (PNF) depuis le printemps dernier, comme le relaie Libération. Une enquête a été ouverte pour "corruption active et passive privée commise en bande organisée". Dans le détail, les investigations se portent sur "la rémunération d'intermédiaires lors d'investissements sur les actifs cotés et non cotés, pour des prestations suspectées d'être fictives, et ayant donné lieu à des rétrocommissions".
Les différentes enquêtes lancées s'interrogent sur les liens entre la direction générale et un intermédiaire, Jean-Pierre Thomas. Ils auraient été sous-estimés par Thomas Saunier, d'après les administrateurs de Malakoff Humanis. Des dizaines de contacts auraient eu lieu au cours des dernières années, selon des enquêtes internes.
Thomas Saunier ne compte pas se laisser faire
Mediapart parle d'un licenciement au titre de faute grave. Nos confrères précisent que Thomas Saunier conteste ce renvoi et qu'il a d'ores et déjà lancé une procédure devant les prud'hommes contre Malakoff Humanis.
Éric Vaudaine est, lui, devenu directeur général par intérim du groupe. Thomas Saunier a été d'abord aux commandes de Malakoff Médéric qui a ensuite fusionné avec Humanis. Le groupe, acteur majeur de la complémentaire santé et de la prévoyance, compte plus de 10 000 salariés.

Visé depuis le printemps par une enquête du Parquet national financier pour corruption privée en bande organisée, le deuxième groupe de protection sociale français se sépare de son directeur général. Au cœur du dossier figure Thomas Vendôme Investment, la société de conseil de l’ancien député Jean-Pierre Thomas, qui a obtenu plus de 22 millions d’euros de commissions auprès des gérants retenus par Malakoff Humanis. Éric Vaudaine, directeur général délégué, assure l’intérim.
Des échanges « occasionnels » : c’est ainsi que Thomas Saunier qualifiait auprès de Mediapart ses relations avec Jean-Pierre Thomas. Les enquêtes internes de Malakoff Humanis ont relevé des dizaines de contacts entre les deux hommes ces dernières années, d’après l’AFP. Réuni vendredi 20 novembre, le conseil d’administration de l’association sommitale, l’instance paritaire qui coiffe le groupe et où siègent patronat et syndicats, a « décidé à l’unanimité de mettre fin au mandat » de son directeur général, selon un message adressé aux salariés que l’agence a pu consulter.
À LIRE AUSSI
Malakoff Humanis croque Mon Petit Placement pour séduire les jeunes épargnants
Le communiqué diffusé dans l’après-midi ne donne aucun motif. Le message interne, signé par le président du conseil, Yves Laqueille (Medef), et par son vice-président, Alain Gautron (FO), reconnaît que « les derniers mois ont pu être éprouvants et générer des interrogations, parfois de l’inquiétude ». Le grief, l’AFP l’a recueilli : les administrateurs reprochent à leur dirigeant d’avoir minimisé devant eux ses liens avec l’intermédiaire au cœur de l’enquête judiciaire.
À LIRE AUSSI
Nestlé vire son Directeur Général pour une « relation amoureuse avec une subordonnée »
Le reproche touche à la loyauté envers le conseil, dans un dossier où rien n’a filtré, à ce stade, sur l’existence ou non de pratiques délictueuses, souligne l’agence. Aucune poursuite n’est annoncée. Thomas Saunier, 59 ans, affirme n’avoir rien su des relations entre son groupe et Jean-Pierre Thomas. Les deux hommes se connaissent de longue date : ils se sont croisés chez Generali, où le consultant siégeait au conseil d’administration quand le futur patron de Malakoff appartenait au comité de direction générale, a raconté Jean-Pierre Thomas à L’Argus de l’assurance. En juin encore, Malakoff Humanis décrivait à Mediapart des relations « strictement professionnelles » entre son directeur général et le consultant. Les partenaires sociaux n’ont donc pas attendu la justice pour trancher.
Les liens passaient aussi par le siège du groupe. Jean-Pierre Thomas préside le Cercle de l’épargne, un think tank dont Malakoff Humanis est devenu l’actionnaire de référence en janvier 2026 et qu’il hébergeait dans ses locaux parisiens, d’après Mediapart. Le groupe a coupé ces liens dans l’attente de la fin des enquêtes.
Thomas Vendôme Investment, l’intermédiaire des gérants
Ancien député, ancien trésorier du Parti républicain, passé par la gestion d’actifs de Lazard, Jean-Pierre Thomas, 69 ans, préside et détient seul Thomas Vendôme Investment (TVI). Sa société de conseil a réalisé 7,5 millions d’euros de chiffre d’affaires et 5,5 millions d’euros de bénéfice en 2025, d’après Mediapart. Le site d’investigation décrit un consultant devenu, depuis l’arrivée de Thomas Saunier chez Malakoff Médéric en 2016, un intermédiaire clé entre le groupe et au moins cinq sociétés de gestion : Sienna, Siparex, Gemway Assets, Lazard et Edmond de Rothschild, qui géraient ensemble plusieurs milliards d’euros pour son compte.
Fin septembre, Mediapart a publié de nouveaux documents selon lesquels TVI a obtenu contractuellement plus de 22 millions d’euros de commissions de la part des gérants retenus par Malakoff Humanis. Ces gérants rémunéraient l’apporteur d’affaires sur les mandats confiés par le groupe. Siparex, l’un d’eux, explique recourir régulièrement à des intermédiaires pour compléter ses équipes commerciales. Reste à savoir ce que TVI fournissait en échange : c’est la réalité de ces prestations que vérifie la justice.
Le cas de Sienna Gestion éclaire ce circuit. Cette société de gestion n’est autre que l’ancienne Malakoff Humanis Gestion d’Actifs, qui gérait 21 milliards d’euros fin 2021. Le 16 mars 2022, le groupe en cède 66,65 % à Sienna, filiale du holding belge GBL, et n’en conserve qu’un tiers. Depuis 2022, Sienna Gestion a versé 6 millions d’euros de commissions à TVI, a chiffré en octobre Alain Gautron auprès de News Assurances Pro, en annonçant que Malakoff Humanis en exigerait le remboursement, ces paiements étant jugés injustifiés. Entre-temps, le groupe a racheté sa société de gestion : sa participation est passée de 33,36 % à 99,35 %, une opération autorisée par l’Autorité de la concurrence le 26 janvier et finalisée fin mai. Malakoff Humanis réclame ainsi à l’intermédiaire l’argent versé par une filiale qu’il contrôle de nouveau.
Corruption privée en bande organisée
Le 16 juin, les enquêteurs de la Brigade financière anticorruption ont perquisitionné le siège de Malakoff Humanis, rue Laffitte, à Paris, puis entendu Thomas Saunier et Jean-Pierre Thomas. Les bureaux parisiens de TVI ont, eux aussi, été perquisitionnés. Ils agissaient dans le cadre d’une enquête préliminaire, conduite par le parquet sans juge d’instruction, ouverte au printemps par le Parquet national financier (PNF) pour « corruption active et passive privée commise en bande organisée ». Une source judiciaire en a résumé l’objet : la rémunération d’intermédiaires lors d’investissements dans des actifs cotés et non cotés, pour des prestations « suspectées d’être fictives ayant donné lieu à rétrocommissions », c’est-à-dire à des sommes reversées en sous-main. Cinq mois plus tard, aucune mise en cause formelle n’a été rendue publique, et toutes les personnes citées sont présumées innocentes.
Le groupe tient dans ce dossier une position double. Visé par les perquisitions, il s’est aussi porté plaignant le 24 juin pour préserver ses intérêts, en récusant « fermement l’existence de toute rétrocommission ». Cette plainte le range du côté des victimes potentielles d’un intermédiaire, ligne que prolonge sa demande de remboursement des 6 millions d’euros versés par Sienna Gestion. Le 8 septembre, il assurait encore qu’« à ce jour, aucun fait de corruption n’a été établi ».
Jean-Pierre Thomas conteste tout autant. Dans un entretien à L’Argus de l’assurance, en octobre, il réfute toute rétrocommission, assume avoir défendu les produits des sociétés de gestion qu’il représentait et dénonce une « opération politique » visant Thomas Saunier, dont TVI serait la « victime collatérale ». Sa défense renvoie la question vers le donneur d’ordre. Le 4 novembre, il la condensait dans L’Agefi : « Il n’y a pas de dossier Thomas Vendôme Investment mais un dossier Malakoff Humanis ».
De l’ACPR au vote unanime
L’affaire est partie du superviseur. Des questions de l’Autorité de contrôle prudentiel et de résolution (ACPR), le gendarme des banques et des assureurs adossé à la Banque de France, ont conduit le groupe à lancer de sa propre initiative, en avril, une enquête interne. Il dit y avoir découvert qu’une partie des sociétés de gestion qu’il avait sélectionnées rémunéraient TVI.
Les 24 et 29 juillet, les conseils de la SGAM (société de groupe d’assurance mutuelle, la structure de tête contrôlée par l’ACPR) et de l’association sommitale adoptent à l’unanimité un plan de remédiation en six points. Le premier impose aux sociétés de gestion une clause de transparence sur les intermédiaires qu’elles rémunèrent au titre des portefeuilles du groupe ; un autre prévoit d’étudier des actions en justice contre des intermédiaires, des gérants ou d’autres prestataires. Deux missions forensiques, c’est-à-dire d’enquête comptable et financière, sont lancées : l’une prolonge l’enquête interne, l’autre porte sur les risques de corruption, de conflits d’intérêts et de favoritisme. Confiées à PwC et DLA Piper, elles passent au crible sept téraoctets de documents, selon News Assurances Pro. Leurs conclusions sont attendues d’ici à la fin de l’année.
Le soutien des administrateurs s’est défait en dix semaines. Le 9 septembre, Alain Gautron assurait à News Assurances Pro que le conseil restait derrière son directeur général, tandis que des administrateurs, dont ceux de la CGT, mettaient en cause son honorabilité. Trois semaines plus tard tombaient les documents de Mediapart sur les commissions de TVI. Le 15 octobre, le conseil de l’association sommitale « constate que la confiance envers le directeur général est ébranlée » et renvoie la décision à « début novembre », après une restitution des enquêteurs forensiques devant le conseil de la SGAM. Le vote est intervenu le 20 novembre. Alain Gautron cosigne, cette fois, le message qui annonce l’éviction.
Un intérim, des comptes à solder
L’intérim revient à Éric Vaudaine, 48 ans, nommé à l’unanimité après avis du comité des rémunérations et de nomination. Polytechnicien passé par Roland Berger et Generali, il a rejoint Malakoff Médéric en 2017 comme directeur des systèmes d’information, avant de devenir en 2021 directeur général délégué, chargé notamment des marchés, des opérations d’assurance et de la retraite complémentaire. Aucun successeur n’est désigné.
Les milliards confiés aux gérants sont ceux d’un acteur central de la protection sociale des salariés. Malakoff Humanis a réalisé 8,37 milliards d’euros de chiffre d’affaires en assurance en 2025 et emploie 10 500 salariés. Premier pilier de la fédération Agirc-Arrco, le régime de retraite complémentaire des salariés du privé, il a versé en 2025 45 milliards d’euros d’allocations de retraite complémentaire à 6,3 millions de retraités. Thomas Saunier avait bâti cet ensemble : arrivé en 2016 à la tête de Malakoff Médéric, il avait conduit la fusion avec Humanis, effective le 1er janvier 2019.
Sa sortie s’annonce contentieuse. Une fois révoqué son mandat social, sa fonction de dirigeant, reste son contrat de travail : d’après Mediapart, une procédure de licenciement pour faute grave a été engagée contre lui, ce que le communiqué du groupe ne mentionne pas. Le même site fait état d’une contestation déjà portée par Thomas Saunier devant le conseil de prud’hommes.

Following the November 15, 2026 close of public consultation on Announcement [2026] No. 48, China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology are enforcing immediate interim pre-export registration across 40 technologies proposed for addition to the national export-control catalogue, compelling international research universities, cross-border joint institutes, and technology-transfer offices to audit outbound data transfers and collaborative intellectual property arrangements.
Scope of the 40 Controlled Technologies
The regulatory transition, initiated formally on November 16, 2026, marks the operational shift from public notice to active administrative gatekeeping. Jointly promulgated by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) Bureau of Industry Security and Export Control and the Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) under Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, the initiative updates the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export. While formal Catalogue additions were open for public comment through mid-November, Chinese trade authorities enacted a mandatory pre-export filing obligation that took immediate effect upon publication.
The 40 targeted technologies expand oversight across three strategic domains. Regulators divided the technologies into two legal tiers: 14 technologies are prohibited from export, imposing an absolute ban on cross-border transfer, while 26 technologies are restricted from export, requiring administrative licensing reviews.
Artificial intelligence accounts for 23 of the 40 items, targeting foundation model parameters, large language model weights, autonomous agent architectures, intelligent computing clusters, and automated vulnerability discovery tools. The remaining items cover 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies—focusing on polysilicon crystallization, wafer slicing, and high-efficiency solar cells—and 5 biomanufacturing technologies encompassing cell and gene therapies, small nucleic acid platforms, and pathogen genetic modification methods.
Technical Thresholds, Prohibitions, and Sourced Specifications
The regulatory schedule establishes concrete technical thresholds to distinguish between prohibited systems, restricted technologies subject to licensing, and unencumbered commercial activities.
For large language models, restricted status applies when a model satisfies any of three quantitative tests: training compute reaching or exceeding 10²⁶ floating-point operations (FLOPs), total model parameters reaching or exceeding 2 trillion, or global top-10 performance on recognized public benchmarks. When a model crosses these thresholds, restrictions attach to model weights, training checkpoints, architecture design documents, and optimization know-how.
Crucially, the rules establish explicit carve-outs. Technologies that have entered the public domain through open-source repository releases or published peer-reviewed academic literature are expressly excluded. Furthermore, MOFCOM clarified that providing foreign end-users with remote access to models hosted on domestic Chinese servers via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) portals, mobile applications, or lightweight on-device runtimes does not constitute a technology export. An export occurs only when model weights, code, or custodial infrastructure are physically transferred or deployed on foreign infrastructure.
In biomanufacturing, authorities introduced a distinction between platform ownership and product-specific licensing. The export prohibition applies exclusively to outbound assignments of intellectual property ownership over reusable foundational platforms. Cross-border out-licensing agreements involving specific therapeutic drug candidates remain eligible for streamlined administrative reviews and prospective automatic licensing, provided that underlying platform intellectual property remains domiciled in China.
Evolution of China’s Technology Export Control Regime
The enforcement of Announcement [2026] No. 48 represents the most substantial structural revision to China’s technology export controls since August 2020. China maintains two parallel statutory frameworks governing cross-border transfers. The dual-use export control regime, administered under the Export Control Law of 2020, governs tangible items, software, and technical data with dual civilian and military utility. In contrast, the technology-trade regime, established under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, regulates commercial transfers of intellectual property, proprietary know-how, and industrial contracts.
The Catalogue was established in 2001 and revised in 2008 and 2020. The 2020 amendments added personalized recommendation algorithms and speech synthesis. The 2026 revisions expand this conceptual foundation to foundational compute infrastructure, synthetic biology platforms, and renewable energy manufacturing.
International regulatory divergence forms the broader context for these measures. As Western jurisdictions expand export controls through instruments such as the United States Export Control Reform Act, semiconductor equipment restrictions, and outbound investment screening, Chinese authorities have modernized their legal architecture. The November 2026 interim measures establish a statutory perimeter designed to prevent the unauthorized transfer of critical technological capabilities developed with domestic funding or proprietary subsidies.
Legal and Industry Reaction to Interim Enforcement
International trade counsel and industry research bodies have evaluated institutional exposure under the interim rules. Legal practitioners at Baker McKenzie observed that immediate interim registration creates an enforceable compliance obligation before the final Catalogue is codified into law. Trade attorneys noted that while registration does not constitute formal export approval, failure to complete pre-export filings before transferring controlled code, data, or technical assistance exposes institutions to administrative penalties under Chinese foreign trade law.
Technical governance analysts at the Cloud Security Alliance highlighted the sophistication of the quantitative criteria, noting that compute thresholds at 10²⁶ FLOPs align with international safety evaluation benchmarks. The organization stressed that separating API-based service access from localized model weight deployments offers vital operational clarity, allowing multinational software ecosystems to operate across Chinese borders so long as model custody remains inside domestic server facilities.
In life sciences, legal specialists at Morgan Lewis emphasized that multinational pharmaceutical developers must conduct immediate portfolio reviews. Corporate acquirers and licensees were advised to structure licensing transactions as product-specific grants rather than platform acquisitions, ensuring that deal documents explicitly separate specific drug candidates from reusable screening platforms to avoid triggering mandatory export prohibitions.
Cross-border investment advisors at Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman warned that interim registration reaches beyond conventional technology sales. The firm highlighted that corporate mergers, equity acquisitions, or corporate restructuring transactions that result in a foreign entity acquiring actual control over a domestic Chinese entity holding controlled technologies constitute an export event requiring pre-closing registration with provincial commerce bureaus.
Operational Impact for Universities, Joint Institutes, and Tech-Transfer Offices
The enforcement of interim registration imposes direct compliance obligations on international higher education institutions, Sino-foreign cooperative universities, and academic research centres. Academic administrators overseeing cross-border programmes must reconcile open research principles with tightening regulatory oversight. Institutional compliance leadership, particularly a university’s research security team, must establish structured screening mechanisms to ensure academic projects do not inadvertently violate export mandates.
Universities operating cooperative joint institutes in China face specific operational considerations. While open academic publishing remains exempt, collaborative laboratory work that involves sharing unpublished artificial intelligence model checkpoints, training datasets, or proprietary biological screening assays falls squarely within interim registration parameters. Research institutions handling advanced machine learning algorithms must review guidelines for export control and AI to prevent the unauthorized transfer of proprietary weights or specialized agent tools.
University technology-transfer offices (TTOs) and sponsored research offices must audit active licensing and collaboration agreements. Under Announcement [2026] No. 48, four operational triggers require immediate registration on the MOFCOM trade portal: outbound assignment of intellectual property ownership; licensing domestic proprietary technology for overseas utilization; corporate changes where the ownership or actual controller of domestic intellectual property shifts to a foreign entity; and specific administrative directives issued by commerce authorities.
When drafting cross-border research agreements, institutional negotiators must evaluate whether their transactional structure constitutes a collaborative development contract or a material transfer. Research administrators must examine the contractual differences between a research collaboration agreement and a material transfer agreement, ensuring that data-sharing provisions, biological sample transfers, and computational resource allocations do not promise the transfer of prohibited platform assets or unregistered restricted methodologies.
Implementation Milestones and Next Steps
With the public comment window concluded, Chinese authorities are consolidating feedback on the 40 proposed technology definitions, with formal promulgation of the revised Catalogue expected in early 2027. In the intervening period, the interim registration system remains fully enforceable across all provincial commerce departments.
Exporters, research institutes, and enterprise legal teams must submit registrations via the MOFCOM Unified Business Platform Technology Trade Management Information Application (`https://ecomp.mofcom.gov.cn`). Filings require detailed institutional data, identification of foreign recipients, end-use documentation, technical parameter descriptions, and projected transaction valuations. Transactions initiated prior to October 16, 2026, but not yet concluded, must complete retroactive registration prior to final closing.
Research administrators, technology-transfer officers, and multinational legal counsel should immediately implement a three-step compliance audit: catalog all active cross-border collaborative research projects touching artificial intelligence, photovoltaics, or biomanufacturing; screen project technical parameters against the 10²⁶ FLOPs and novel-target thresholds; and adjust contractual licensing provisions to safeguard foundational platform ownership within domestic legal jurisdictions.

ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.
As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.
Many countries were not buying it.
For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.
The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.
The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.
Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.
In 2022, the U.N. conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.
Since then, international collaboration on climate issues has declined amid increased conflict, rising oil and gas prices and economic insecurity. The talks in Turkey ran two days beyond the scheduled end without reaching broad agreement on potential next steps, an outcome that won’t kill the global effort but is widely viewed as a serious setback.
But compromise for the sake of consensus is not enough, said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of the Environment.
“We will not be forced to accept false solutions,” she said. “We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.” As written, she added, the Antalya Pact undermines her country’s security and threatens its future.
“People are dying, seas are rising and ecosystems are collapsing,” Jetn̄il-Kijiner said. “Are we so divorced from reality that we take backward steps, even as overshoot threatens to overtake us? To accept this deal would be a betrayal to the Marshallese people.”
It’s not the first time Pacific Island nations threatened by rising seas have objected to the outcome at one of the United Nations’ annual conferences. During the 2023 U.N. talks in Dubai, a final text was adopted even though a delegation representing 39 small island developing states objected because they were still outside the plenary meeting, trying to coordinate their position.
But in Antalya, the divide ran much deeper. The economically powerful and politically influential European Union, representing 28 member countries, also rejected the proposed agreement.
Ireland’s climate, energy and environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the European countries formally objected to the cover decision because it fell short of what the global climate crisis demands.
“We will not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the key driver of climate change, and not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” said O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU during Ireland’s rotating presidency.
Egypt and Brazil, hosts of the U.N. climate talks in 2023 and 2025, also criticized the text proposed by COP31 president Kurum of Turkey and Chris Bowen of Australia, president of the conference negotiations.

Liliam Beatris Chagas de Moura, director for climate at Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said she was disappointed that this year’s conference did not sustain the momentum from last year’s talks in her country.
Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator with the Saudi Arabian energy ministry, said the 22-member League of Arab States supported the proposed Antalya Pact. He criticized developed countries for using up most of the global carbon budget, the amount of fossil fuels that can be burned without overheating the planet, and then asking developing countries to give up the very energy sources that fueled their own growth.
Ayoub condemned some countries’ opposition to including references to carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture and storage in the pact, calling their resistance to those technologies unscientific.
Carbon capture and storage are not close to being deployed fast enough “to keep 1.5 degrees within reach,” he said, referring to the long-term goal of limiting the average global temperature increase established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table, and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances.”
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said he was “deeply disappointed” that the talks ended without consensus on an overarching agreement.
“But this setback does not change the facts,” he said. “Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis. We can’t put out the fire while pouring fuel on it.”

a137.texte: Dans les grottes de Rising Star, en Afrique du Sud, les squelettes d’Homo naledi réservent une surprise. L’analyse des protéines de leur émail dentaire suggère que les individus retrouvés seraient tous de sexe féminin. Un résultat inattendu qui intrigue les spécialistes de cette ancienne espèce humaine.

L’ESSENTIEL
- La crise d’Ormuz a affecté les prix du gaz dans l’Union européenne, alors qu’une faible part du gaz importé par l’UE transite par ce détroit.
- Derrière ce paradoxe se trouve la profonde transformation du marché gazier européen depuis 2022, à la suite de la guerre en Ukraine.
- L’UE s’est largement tournée vers le gaz naturel liquéfié. Si le risque de rupture physique a reculé, celui d’une flambée des prix demeure.
Au printemps 2026, la crise du détroit d’Ormuz a fait flamber les prix du gaz en Europe. Pourtant, moins de 10 % du gaz naturel liquéfié (GNL) importé par l’Union européenne (UE) transitait par ce passage du golfe Persique en 2025. Comment un choc qui frappe d’abord l’Asie, principale destination des cargaisons de GNL empruntant cette route, peut-il autant affecter les Européens ? La réponse tient à la transformation du marché gazier depuis 2022.
L’UE a réussi à se passer de l’essentiel du gaz russe acheminé par gazoduc, sans rupture majeure d’approvisionnement. Mais en se tournant vers le GNL transporté par bateau, elle s’est davantage exposée aux tensions du marché mondial. Le risque de rupture physique a reculé ; celui d’une flambée des prix demeure.
Nouvelles portes d’entrée du gaz
La recomposition est considérable au regard de la forte dépendance de l’Europe au gaz russe que nous soulignions dans une précédente étude publiée en 2022. Entre 2021 et 2025, les livraisons russes par gazoduc à l’UE ont chuté de 87 %, passant de 1 535 à 206 térawattheures (TWh). Les livraisons des autres fournisseurs par gazoduc sont, quant à elles, restées globalement stables. La montée du GNL et le recul de la demande ont permis d’absorber la baisse des livraisons russes.
Read more: Ce que la crise d’Ormuz a changé (ou non) au monde de l’énergie
La part du GNL dans les entrées de gaz de l’Union est ainsi passée de 20 % en 2021 à 46 % en 2025. Alors que le gaz russe arrivait principalement par les gazoducs de l’est, le GNL est désormais acheminé vers les terminaux des façades atlantique et méditerranéenne. Selon nos calculs, le centre de gravité des entrées de gaz s’est déplacé de 329 kilomètres vers le sud-ouest entre 2020 et 2025 (graphique 1). Ce basculement n’a toutefois pas été improvisé. Dès janvier 2009, un différend entre la Russie et l’Ukraine avait interrompu pendant près de deux semaines le transit par lequel passaient alors environ 80 % des importations européennes de gaz russe. Cette crise avait conduit l’Europe à renforcer ses interconnexions et les possibilités d’inverser les flux, avant de compléter ces infrastructures après 2022.
Graphique 1. Points d’entrée physiques du gaz dans l’Union européenne : 2021 et 2025. La taille des points représente les volumes annuels.
Source : ENTSOG et GIE/ALSI (calculs des auteurs)
Cette transformation ne concerne pas seulement les modes de transport. Contrairement au gaz acheminé par gazoduc, les cargaisons de GNL peuvent être réorientées d’un marché à l’autre en fonction des prix.
Une plaque tournante européenne
La circulation du gaz a elle aussi changé. En 2021, les grands flux partaient de l’est vers le centre et le sud du continent. En 2025, ils provenaient davantage des façades maritimes de l’ouest. La France illustre cette inversion. En 2025, 15,4 % du gaz entrant pour la première fois dans l’UE passe par la France, contre 9,8 % en 2021, ce qui en fait la deuxième porte d’entrée après l’Italie. Cette hausse tient au GNL, dont les volumes sont passés de 182 à 329 TWh, tandis que les entrées par gazoduc restaient stables.
La France est également devenue ré expéditrice nette : son solde de transit est passé de – 97 TWh en 2021 à + 145 TWh en 2025 (graphique 2). Elle alimente la Suisse, relais vers l’Italie, et la Belgique, dont l’Allemagne est le premier débouché.
L’Allemagne, qui était autrefois la plaque tournante des livraisons russes, reçoit désormais davantage de ses voisins européens. La France ne l’a pas simplement remplacée : le système s’organise autour de plusieurs portes maritimes plutôt que d’un axe dominant. En redistribuant du gaz importé, la France contribue ainsi à la sécurité d’approvisionnement de ses voisins.
Graphique 2. Évolution du solde net de transit de la France, de l’Allemagne, de la Belgique et des Pays-Bas (TWh/an, 2020–2025)
Source : ENTSOG (calculs des auteurs)
Une diversification réelle, mais de nouveaux risques
L’UE a incontestablement diversifié ses fournisseurs (graphique 3). Selon nos calculs, la part de la Russie dans les entrées primaires de gaz de l’Union, GNL compris, est en effet passée de 48 % en 2020 à 16 % en 2025. Sur la même période, celle des États-Unis a progressé de 5 % à 27 %. La Norvège demeure un fournisseur essentiel, avec environ un quart des entrées.
La France présente, en 2025, un profil particulier : 33 % de ses entrées proviennent de Norvège, 34 % des États-Unis et encore 20 % de Russie, désormais sous forme de GNL. La sortie du gaz russe n’y est donc pas achevée, même si l’interdiction européenne du GNL russe doit s’étendre aux contrats de long terme au 1er janvier 2027.
Il ne s’agit pas pour autant d’une dépendance états-unienne identique à celle qui prévalait envers la Russie. Le gaz par gazoduc dépend d’infrastructures fixes ; une cargaison de GNL peut changer de destination. Mais lorsque l’offre se tend, les acheteurs européens sont en concurrence avec les acheteurs asiatiques. Les contrats de long terme sécurisent des volumes sans éliminer tous les risques. En 2024, les achats au comptant représentaient un peu plus du quart du GNL importé dans l’UE, exposant les acheteurs à la concurrence asiatique.
Graphique 3. Évolution des principales origines des entrées de gaz de l’Union européenne (en %, 2020–2025)
Source : ENTSOG, GIE/ALSI et Bloomberg (calculs des auteurs)
Une solidarité encore imparfaite
Entre 2019 et 2025, les capacités européennes de regazéification ont augmenté de 48 %, mais leur taux d’utilisation n’était que de 42 % en 2024 et 51 % en 2025. Le paradoxe n’est qu’apparent. En 2022, au moment de remplacer le gaz russe, les terminaux du nord-ouest de l’Europe étaient saturés et l’Allemagne n’en possédait aucun ; les capacités disponibles se trouvaient surtout en Espagne, loin des besoins. Il a donc fallu construire là où le gaz manquait, et ces nouveaux terminaux sont entrés en service au moment où la consommation européenne reculait. Cette surcapacité est assumée : elle a été conçue comme une « assurance stratégique », dimensionnée pour les pointes d’hiver et les crises, non pour une année ordinaire.
Le cas de l’Espagne est différent. Elle dispose des plus grandes capacités de regazéification du continent, mais n’en utilisait que 28 % en 2025. Construits dans les années 2000 pour son seul marché, en prévision d’une demande qui n’est jamais venue, ses terminaux n’ont pas été pensés comme une porte d’entrée de l’Europe, ce dont témoigne l’étroitesse des interconnexions pyrénéennes.
Le stockage présente la même asymétrie. Au creux de mars 2026, les réserves européennes n’étaient remplies qu’à 28 % : environ 22 % en France et en Allemagne, moins de 5 % aux Pays-Bas, contre près de 57 % en Espagne. Or les réserves les mieux garnies ne sont pas toujours facilement accessibles aux voisins. Obliger à remplir les stocks renforce la sécurité, mais peut renchérir les achats. L’assouplissement des objectifs en 2025 reflète cet arbitrage entre coût et précaution.
Les prix européens sont désormais plus sensibles au marché asiatique
Afin de compléter l’analyse des flux physiques, notre étude examine également les liens entre les trois prix de référence du gaz : TTF européen, JKM asiatique et Henry Hub états-unien, de 2015 à 2026. En recourant à diverses méthodes économétriques, nous analysons la synchronisation des variations quotidiennes des prix à terme et la transmission des chocs.
Après février 2022, la corrélation moyenne entre les variations quotidiennes du TTF et du JKM est passée de 0,110 à 0,185, soit une hausse relative de 69 %. Nos estimations montrent également que la part des fluctuations imprévues du marché européen expliquée par les chocs asiatiques est passée de 5,9 % à 15,7 %. La transmission inverse s’est aussi renforcée : l’interdépendance entre les deux marchés s’est donc accrue dans les deux sens.
À l’inverse, le prix états-unien reste relativement déconnecté. Depuis 2022, les installations américaines de liquéfaction fonctionnent à 93 à 98 % de leur capacité, ce qui limite les possibilités d’augmenter rapidement les exportations lorsque les prix européens ou asiatiques s’envolent.
Par ailleurs, la production américaine de gaz de schiste a pu accompagner la croissance des exportations sans hausse durable des prix intérieurs. Le Henry Hub réagit donc peu aux tensions entre l’Europe et l’Asie. De fait, la corrélation entre les marchés européen et états-unien n’a que très légèrement augmenté après 2022, d’environ 6 %, une évolution sans commune mesure avec celle observée entre l’Europe et l’Asie. Le principal changement concerne donc bien l’axe Europe-Asie.
Ormuz, un révélateur de cette nouvelle vulnérabilité
La crise d’Ormuz en offre l’illustration. Environ un cinquième du commerce mondial de GNL transitait par le détroit, principalement vers l’Asie. L’exposition européenne directe était faible, mais les prix ont fortement augmenté des deux côtés. En mars 2026, le prix européen TTF a dépassé 60 euros par mégawattheure, alors qu’il se situait autour de 30 euros avant le choc. Plus récemment, au cours de la première semaine de novembre 2026, il s’établissait en moyenne à un peu plus de 90 euros par mégawattheure.
Privés de cargaisons du Golfe, les acheteurs asiatiques se reportent sur d’autres fournisseurs et concurrencent les Européens. Le prix des cargaisons disponibles augmente. Ainsi, même lorsque ses approvisionnements directs sont relativement peu affectés, l’Europe peut subir les conséquences d’un choc lointain transmis par les prix.
Les limites de la diversification
Cette évolution ne remet pas en cause les bénéfices de la diversification, mais en révèle les limites. Disposer de terminaux ne suffit pas si les cargaisons sont rares ou trop chères, tandis que les stocks disponibles ne profitent pas nécessairement aux pays qui en ont le plus besoin. De même, les contrats de long terme peuvent sécuriser les approvisionnements, sans éliminer tous les risques de perturbation de l’offre.
Ces nouvelles vulnérabilités appellent une meilleure coordination européenne, tant en matière de diversification des fournisseurs que de gestion des stocks et d’interconnexions. Elles soulignent également la nécessité de renforcer la résilience des industries fortement consommatrices de gaz, notamment la chimie, face à la volatilité des prix.
La réduction de la dépendance au gaz russe constitue un progrès réel. Elle n’a toutefois pas supprimé les risques, mais en a profondément modifié la nature. La sécurité énergétique européenne ne se mesure donc plus seulement à la capacité de l’Union à garantir ses approvisionnements, mais aussi à celle d’en limiter les conséquences économiques lorsque les tensions sur le marché mondial du gaz provoquent une flambée des prix.

Coco Gauff et les États-Unis matent la Hongrie et restent dans le groupe mondial de Billie Jean King Cup

depeches.titre: Un trophée de plus à son palmarès : avec sa victoire lors des Finales ATP, où se situe Carlos Alcaraz parmi les plus grands collectionneurs ?
depeches.resume: En s'imposant aux Finales ATP face à Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz a remporté un des seuls grands titres qu'il ne comptait pas encore à son palmarès. Il se rapproche ainsi des collectionneurs les plus déterminés de l'histoire.

depeches.resume: À peine plus d'un an après le début de leur association, Albano Olivetti et Théo Arribagé ont remporté les Finales ATP dimanche à Turin face à la paire Pavic-Arevalo (3-6, 7-6 [2], 10-6). Le duo rêve désormais de Coupe Davis et de Grands Chelems.

depeches.titre: Carlos Alcaraz s'offre un premier titre aux Finales ATP de Turin en dominant Alexander Zverev

depeches.titre: Albano Olivetti et Théo Arribagé après leur titre aux Finales ATP de Turin : « C'est un truc de fou »
